title: Centre-Restart Conversion Simulation
primarySkill: Converting centre-clearance possession into an effective forward entry.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to win, receive or recover possession from a centre restart and convert it into a controlled scoring opportunity while maintaining protection against turnover.
groundSize: Centre square to the attacking goal, using approximately half to two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position two teams around a centre restart, including rucks, inside midfielders, wings, half-forwards, key forwards and defenders.
Begin each repetition with a ball-up or controlled ruck contest in the centre circle.
The attacking team scores through a goal, behind or marked possession inside 30 metres.
The defending team scores by winning possession and moving the football beyond the centre square or through designated wide exit gates.
Place one spare football with the coach for rapid resets.
Rotate starting midfield combinations every three to four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach restarts play with a centre ball-up.
Both teams contest possession using their normal centre-restart structures.
The team winning the clearance attempts to create a purposeful forward entry rather than immediately kicking without assessing options.
Forwards may lead at the football, hold deeper space or create separation for a teammate.
If the defending team wins possession, play continues live as it attempts to exit through the centre or wide gates.
Award three points for a goal, two points for a marked possession inside 30 metres and one point for an uncontested inside-50 possession.
Award the defensive team two points for a clean turnover and successful exit.
Stop the repetition after a score, defensive exit, stoppage lasting more than five seconds or the football leaves the designated area.
Reset quickly and repeat from the centre.
coachingPoints: Midfielders must scan before the ruck contest and understand the likely hit zone.
The first possession should create time and space for the next disposal rather than forcing an immediate clearance.
Outside midfielders must hold width until possession is established.
Forwards should coordinate leads so that multiple players do not attack the same space.
The ball carrier should identify whether the best option is a direct corridor entry, a wide release or a controlled possession.
Players behind the football must protect against a turnover and immediate counterattack.
Communication must begin before the ball-up and continue through the entire passage.
After a lost clearance, all players must react immediately and defend the next possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether midfielders adjust their starting positions to the nominated or developing hit zone.
Whether the clearance winner has support forward, lateral and behind.
Whether forwards create multiple usable lanes rather than leading into congestion.
Whether the inside-50 kick is selected according to pressure and forward positioning.
Whether defenders and midfielders react immediately when possession changes.
Whether the team maintains a balanced structure behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders all chase the football into the same space.
commonErrors.correction: Assign clear hit-zone, receiver and defensive-side roles before each restart.

commonErrors.error: The clearance is kicked forward without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require the ball carrier to identify a target or release option before disposing.

commonErrors.error: Forwards lead toward the same corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate separate lead lanes and demand early communication.

commonErrors.error: Wings collapse too early into the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the team has clearly won or lost possession.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after losing the clearance.
commonErrors.correction: Continue every repetition until the opposition exits or a stoppage is called.

progressions: Allow the defending team to launch a full counterattack toward the opposite goal.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios before each centre restart.
Require the attacking side to use a nominated forward-entry method, then remove the restriction.
Start some repetitions with an unexpected ruck hit or loose football.
Allow coaches to change midfield match-ups between repetitions.
regressions: Begin with an uncontested ruck hit to a nominated midfielder.
Reduce the number of defenders in the forward half.
Limit play to one centre-clearance method at a time.
Use controlled contact and slower resets.
Mark preferred forward-entry lanes with cones.
successIndicators: Establish clear roles before the centre restart.
Win or neutralise first possession without overcommitting.
Create a controlled inside-50 entry from the clearance.
Provide width, depth and forward support.
Generate a shot, mark or strong contest inside 50.
React immediately when the opposition wins possession.
matchApplication: This drill replicates the moments immediately after a centre bounce, when teams must convert a clearance into a scoring opportunity while remaining prepared for an opposition win. It develops the connection between the ruck, midfield, wings and forwards and reinforces the importance of attacking with structure rather than relying on rushed territory kicks.

title: Defensive Kick-In Exit Simulation
primarySkill: Exiting defensive 50 from a kick-in against an organised opposition press.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to create, recognise and execute safe or aggressive defensive-50 exits from a kick-in while responding appropriately to opposition pressure.
groundSize: Defensive goal square to approximately 20 metres beyond the centre of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team to take a kick-in from the goal square.
Organise the opposition in a realistic forward-half press.
Place exit gates near each wing and one central gate beyond defensive 50.
Include defenders, midfielders and high forwards for the exiting team.
The exiting team scores by retaining possession and moving through a gate.
The pressing team scores by forcing a turnover and generating a shot at goal.
Alternate the player taking the kick-in and vary opposition pressing structures.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach signals a behind and places a football in the goal square.
The designated player takes the kick-in while teammates organise their starting shape.
The defending team may play short, run from the square, switch the football or attack a longer target.
The opposition applies a realistic press and attempts to deny obvious exits.
Play continues until the exiting team crosses an exit gate under control, the pressing team scores or the football leaves the area.
Award the exiting team two points for a controlled exit and three points for reaching the central gate without a turnover.
Award the pressing team three points for a goal and two points for a turnover inside 50.
Reset immediately with a different kick-in taker or starting press.
Review the team’s spacing after every three repetitions rather than stopping after every disposal.
coachingPoints: The kick-in taker must scan the entire ground before committing to an option.
Players should create width and depth rather than forming a flat line.
Short options must move defenders and open the next kick, not merely receive the football.
The far-side defender must remain available for a switch.
Players ahead of the football should create strong marking contests and predictable support at ground level.
The team must recognise when the corridor is available and when the safer boundary exit is required.
Players must not all move toward the football at once.
After a turnover, defenders must protect the goal corridor immediately.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The kick-in taker’s scanning and decision speed.
Whether short options create useful angles.
Whether the far side remains occupied for a switch.
Whether marking targets are supported front and square.
Whether players communicate changes in the opposition press.
Whether turnover defence is immediate and organised.

commonErrors.error: All defenders lead toward the same side.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a far-side option and stagger leads at different depths.

commonErrors.error: The kick-in taker chooses the first visible option.
commonErrors.correction: Scan both sides and identify the opposition’s weakest zone before playing on.

commonErrors.error: Short kicks trap the team near the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Use the first short possession to improve angle and open the next disposal.

commonErrors.error: Long targets are isolated.
commonErrors.correction: Position support players at the front, back and ground level of the contest.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to defend after a turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate corridor protection as the first turnover responsibility.

progressions: Allow the pressing team to change between zone, man-on-man and hybrid structures.
Introduce a six-second decision limit for the kick-in.
Require the exiting side to reach inside 50 at the opposite end before scoring.
Add scoreboard scenarios requiring either risk-taking or possession retention.
Begin with the kick-in team temporarily outnumbered.
regressions: Remove one or two opposition forwards from the press.
Freeze the opposition while the kick-in team establishes its initial shape.
Restrict the press to a single known structure.
Increase the width of the exit gates.
Allow the coach to nominate the first receiving option.
successIndicators: Establish a balanced kick-in structure quickly.
Create multiple short, medium and long options.
Recognise and use the open side of the press.
Support long contests at ground level.
Defend the corridor immediately after turnover.
matchApplication: This drill replicates kick-ins against a structured opposition press. It trains defenders and midfielders to create useful space, move the opposition, select the correct level of risk and remain organised if the exit fails.

title: Boundary-Stoppage Territory Simulation
primarySkill: Winning or neutralising a boundary stoppage and improving field position.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to manage boundary stoppages by protecting the defensive side, creating a clean exit when available and gaining territory without exposing the corridor.
groundSize: A boundary channel approximately 70 metres long and 35–45 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a long channel along one boundary.
Position a ruck and three to five stoppage players per team around a boundary throw-in point.
Place supporting wing, half-back and half-forward players outside the immediate stoppage.
Mark a territory line 25 metres in each direction from the starting stoppage.
The attacking team aims to progress toward its scoring end.
The defensive team aims to force the football backward, out of bounds or into a controlled turnover.
Rotate rucks, inside midfielders and outside support roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a boundary throw-in or controlled high toss.
Both teams contest the stoppage using their nominated structures.
The team winning possession attempts to exit forward or release to an outside player.
If no clean release is available, players may use a controlled territory kick or force another stoppage further forward.
The opposition attempts to win possession, trap the football or counter through the inside edge.
Award two points for crossing the forward territory line under possession.
Award one point for creating a repeat stoppage at least 15 metres forward.
Award three points for an opposition turnover followed by a clean inside release.
Continue play through one secondary stoppage before resetting.
Change the starting location and attacking direction regularly.
coachingPoints: Protect the defensive side of the stoppage before attacking the football.
The ruck should hit to space that matches teammate positioning.
Inside players must maintain separation between ball winner, blocker and receiver roles.
Outside players should remain wide enough to be used but close enough to defend.
Territory is valuable when a clean possession exit is unavailable.
Players must avoid blindly handballing into congestion.
The team should recognise when to hold the boundary and when the inside release is safe.
Repeat stoppages require immediate reorganisation.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defensive side is protected before the contest.
The ruck’s connection with inside midfielders.
Whether players maintain distinct stoppage roles.
Whether outside support holds usable width.
The decision between possession, territory and repeat stoppage.
How quickly players reset after the football goes out of bounds.

commonErrors.error: All inside players chase the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign ball-winner, support and defensive-side roles.

commonErrors.error: The ruck hits to an unoccupied area.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm the target zone and receiver before the throw-in.

commonErrors.error: Players force handballs into congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Use territory or absorb the tackle when no clean release exists.

commonErrors.error: Outside players stand too close to the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the football clearly exits.

commonErrors.error: The corridor is exposed after possession is lost.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one player responsible for the inside edge.

progressions: Add a scoreboard consequence for conceding an inside release.
Allow play to continue to goal after a territory-line crossing.
Change the stoppage location between attacking and defensive halves.
Introduce uneven numbers around the stoppage.
Require teams to identify and call their stoppage plan before each repetition.
regressions: Use a controlled ruck hit to a nominated side.
Limit contact around the initial ruck contest.
Pause after the ruck contest to coach player spacing.
successIndicators: Protect the dangerous side of the stoppage.
Maintain clear roles around the contest.
Create or deny clean possession exits.
Gain territory when controlled possession is unavailable.
Support the first disposal outside the stoppage.
matchApplication: Boundary stoppages often determine whether a team gains territory, escapes pressure or concedes access to the corridor. This simulation develops the tactical discipline required to balance possession, territory and defensive protection in realistic field positions.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Half-Back Turnover Attack Simulation
primarySkill: Attacking from a turnover won across half-back.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to recognise a turnover across half-back, secure the first possession and transition into attack before the opposition can restore its defensive structure.
groundSize: From defensive 50 to the attacking goal, using approximately two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position an attacking team inside 50 and a defending team across defensive 50 and half-back.
Place additional midfielders and forwards further up the ground.
The coach begins with a kick or handball directed toward an intercept or contested situation at half-back.
The team winning possession attacks the far goal.
The original attacking team immediately transitions to defence.
Mark a central corridor and two wide channels to assist observation.
Rotate the player receiving the initial turnover opportunity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach delivers the football into a half-back contest or intercept situation.
The defending team attempts to win possession cleanly.
On turnover, the first player must secure the football and identify the fastest safe attacking option.
Teammates spread through the corridor, outside lanes and behind the ball.
The opposition applies immediate transition pressure.
Play continues until a score, turnover, stoppage or defensive rebound.
Award three points for a goal launched from the turnover.
Award two points for a controlled inside-50 entry.
Award the opposition two points for regaining possession before the football crosses the centre.
Reset with a new starting contest.
coachingPoints: The intercepting player should secure possession before attempting an aggressive disposal.
The first receiver must scan forward before automatically moving wide.
Players ahead of the football should accelerate into space immediately after turnover.
The corridor should be used when it is open, not forced when it is defended.
Running support must occur both ahead of and behind the ball carrier.
Forwards should recognise the speed of transition and adjust their leading depth.
Players behind the football must protect against a counter-turnover.
Communication should identify corridor, switch and overlap opportunities.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The quality of the first possession after turnover.
Whether players change from defensive to attacking movement immediately.
Whether the corridor is recognised early.
The timing and angle of supporting runs.
Whether forwards create space for a fast entry.
Whether sufficient players remain behind the football.

commonErrors.error: The intercepting player disposes before securing the football.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the mark or gather, balance and then assess.

commonErrors.error: All players run forward of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one or two connected support players behind possession.

commonErrors.error: The team automatically exits wide.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the corridor first and use width only when it improves the next possession.

commonErrors.error: Forwards lead too early and run out of space.
commonErrors.correction: Match the lead timing to the ball carrier’s ability to advance.

commonErrors.error: Players jog after the turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Demand immediate acceleration during the first three seconds.

progressions: Begin with a more difficult contested spoil rather than a clean intercept.
Add a time limit for reaching inside 50.
Allow the opposition to counterattack fully after a second turnover.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios rewarding either speed or possession retention.
Start with the turnover team temporarily outnumbered.
regressions: Begin with an uncontested intercept mark.
Remove one or two opposition transition defenders.
Mark preferred running lanes with cones.
Allow the first disposal to be unpressured.
Reduce the distance to the scoring end.
successIndicators: Transition from defence to attack immediately.
Connect half-back, midfield and forward lines.
Retain defensive coverage behind the football.
matchApplication: Many scoring opportunities begin with an intercept or ground-ball win across half-back. This drill recreates the brief period when the opposition is out of position and the turnover team must decide whether to attack quickly, switch or retain possession.

title: Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation
primarySkill: Maintaining forward-half pressure while the defending team attempts to exit.
objective: Develop both teams’ ability to execute the competing demands of forward-half lock-in pressure and composed defensive-50 exit play.
groundSize: One half of a full ground, including the goal and approximately 20 metres beyond the centre line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position one team in attack inside its forward half.
Position the opposition in defensive structure with kick-in, marking and ground-level exit options.
Start each repetition with a forward entry, rushed behind, intercept mark or loose football nominated by the coach.
The attacking team scores through normal scoring or repeat possession inside 50.
The defending team scores by exiting beyond the centre line under control.
Mark wide exit gates and a central exit gate.
Rotate team roles after four to six repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach introduces the football into the attacking team’s forward half.
The attacking team attempts to score or lock the football inside 50.
If the defending team wins possession, it immediately attempts to exit through a designated gate.
The attacking team must establish a press without allowing easy corridor access.
If the football is forced out of bounds or into a stoppage, play restarts from that location.
Award the attacking team three points for a goal, two points for a turnover inside 50 and one point for a repeat entry.
Award the defending team three points for a controlled central exit and two points for a wide exit.
Continue each repetition for up to 60 seconds.
Reset after a score, successful exit or time expiry.
Swap roles and compare scoring efficiency.
coachingPoints: The attacking team must apply pressure while preserving its overall shape.
The nearest player pressures the ball carrier while others protect likely exits.
High forwards and midfielders must prevent easy corridor access.
Defenders should create width, depth and multiple exit options.
The first defensive possession should reduce pressure rather than create another contest.
Both teams must react instantly when possession changes.
Ground-level players should anticipate where marking contests will spill.
Communication must identify free players, dangerous exits and switch options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether forward pressure is connected rather than individual.
Whether the press protects central exits.
Whether defenders create usable width and depth.
The quality of the first possession after a turnover.
Whether players continue working after the first exit attempt is stopped.

commonErrors.error: Multiple forwards chase the same ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: One player pressures while others close the next options.

commonErrors.error: The attacking press becomes too narrow.
commonErrors.correction: Hold outside coverage while protecting the corridor.

commonErrors.error: Defenders kick long without support.
commonErrors.correction: Establish ground-level numbers around the marking target.

commonErrors.error: The first defensive possession goes backward without purpose.
commonErrors.correction: Use backward movement only to improve angle or access the far side.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after the first contest.
commonErrors.correction: Continue pressure and support until the football exits or play ends.

progressions: Allow the defending team to continue into a full-ground counterattack.
Change the attacking team’s starting entry quality.
Add a time or scoreboard scenario.
Restrict the defending side to a certain number of uncontested possessions before exiting.
Introduce fatigue by repeating multiple entries without a full reset.
regressions: Reduce the number of attacking press players.
Begin with the defending team in uncontested possession.
Freeze play after the first possession to coach structure.
successIndicators: Create repeat entries or shots from turnovers.
Use the first possession to improve control.
Transition immediately between attack and defence.
matchApplication: This simulation recreates one of the most important tactical contests in Australian football: one team attempting to lock the football in its forward half while the other tries to escape defensive pressure. It trains both systems at the same time and exposes structural weaknesses that isolated drills may not reveal.
relatedDrills: MS-009 – Coach Observation and Feedback Simulation

title: Numerical-Advantage Transition Simulation
primarySkill: Using or defending a temporary numerical advantage during transition.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to recognise and exploit an outnumber during transition while teaching the defending team to delay, protect dangerous space and recover support.
groundSize: A corridor 80–110 metres long and 45–60 metres wide leading toward goal.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create a transition channel from half-back or the centre toward goal.
Arrange attacking groups with a temporary advantage such as four against three, five against four or six against four.
Position recovering players behind the initial play.
Start with a turnover, intercept or loose-ball win.
The attackers attempt to score before the recovering defenders restore equal numbers.
Rotate attackers, initial defenders and recovering defenders.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach starts play by releasing a football to the attacking group.
Attackers transition toward goal with a temporary numerical advantage.
Initial defenders attempt to slow the attack and protect the most dangerous space.
Recovering defenders enter after a three- to five-second delay.
Attackers must decide when to carry, draw, handball, kick or use the spare player.
Play continues until a score, turnover or defensive recovery.
Award three points for a goal before numbers become equal.
Award two points for a controlled shot after defenders recover.
Award the defending team two points for forcing a turnover or delaying the attack for 15 seconds.
Change the numerical advantage and starting field position between repetitions.
coachingPoints: Attackers should identify the spare player before receiving possession.
The ball carrier must commit a defender before releasing the football.
Support players should maintain width and avoid running into the same lane.
The final disposal should be delayed until the scoring option is clear.
Defenders should protect the corridor and force play toward less dangerous space.
The first defender applies pressure while others guard the next options.
Recovering defenders must sprint to useful positions rather than following the football.
Communication must identify the spare attacker and defensive match-ups.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether attackers identify the numerical advantage early.
The spacing between ball carrier and support players.
Whether defenders protect dangerous central space.
The quality and timing of the final disposal.
Whether recovering defenders run to influence the next possession.
Whether attackers remain composed as the advantage reduces.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier releases before drawing a defender.
commonErrors.correction: Carry directly at the defender before disposing.

commonErrors.error: Attackers run in parallel too close together.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain separate lanes and stagger depth.

commonErrors.error: Defenders chase the football and expose goal-side space.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and force play wider.

commonErrors.error: Recovering defenders run behind opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Recover to the next dangerous space or available match-up.

commonErrors.error: Attackers rush the final kick.
commonErrors.correction: Balance, scan and select the highest-percentage scoring option.

progressions: Randomise the numerical advantage before each repetition.
Allow a second wave of attackers or defenders to enter.
Add a scoreboard target requiring a goal rather than a behind.
Begin from different turnover locations.
Permit full contact and live counterattack after a turnover.
regressions: Reduce the length of the transition area.
Begin with the spare player clearly identified.
successIndicators: Maintain width and depth in transition.
Draw defenders before releasing the football.
matchApplication: Temporary numerical advantages occur after turnovers, broken tackles, intercepts and defensive errors. This simulation develops the speed of recognition and decision making required to convert an outnumber while also teaching defenders to delay the attack until support arrives.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Red-Time Quarter Management Simulation
primarySkill: Managing possession, field position and risk during the closing minutes of a quarter.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to adjust its playing method during red time according to the score, field position, possession status and remaining time.
groundSize: Two-thirds to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Use a visible scoreboard and countdown clock.
Prepare multiple scenarios such as leading by four points, trailing by two points or scores level.
Start play from different positions including defensive 50, a boundary stoppage, centre restart or forward-half possession.
Give one team a specific objective based on the scenario.
Coaches should avoid directing every possession once play begins.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the score, time remaining and starting position.
Teams have 20 seconds to communicate their tactical approach.
Play begins live and continues until the clock expires or a decisive score occurs.
The team in front may need to retain possession, gain territory or prevent a dangerous turnover.
The trailing team may need to increase risk, force stoppages or attack the corridor.
Award the scenario win to the team that achieves the required match outcome.
After each repetition, allow players to explain the decisions they made.
Change the score, time and field position.
Rotate leadership responsibility between players.
Complete four to six scenarios.
coachingPoints: Players must know the score and remaining time before the football is restarted.
The team’s level of risk should match the match situation.
Possession retention must still improve field position or remove opposition scoring opportunity.
Boundary use can reduce risk and consume time when leading.
The trailing team must identify when to attack centrally and when to force a stoppage.
Players behind the football must maintain protection against turnover.
Leaders should communicate the plan clearly and repeatedly.
Players must remain composed despite time pressure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players understand the scenario before play begins.
The level of risk selected by each team.
Whether possession is purposeful or merely slow.
Whether players use the boundary and corridor appropriately.
Leadership communication around stoppages and marks.
Whether players maintain structure under time pressure.

commonErrors.error: Players are unaware of the time remaining.
commonErrors.correction: Require leaders to call time and score before every restart.

commonErrors.error: The leading team takes unnecessary corridor risk.
commonErrors.correction: Use safer possession unless a clear high-percentage option exists.

commonErrors.error: The trailing team moves the football too slowly.
commonErrors.correction: Identify earlier where risk must increase.

commonErrors.error: Players retain possession without gaining safety or territory.
commonErrors.correction: Use each disposal to improve field position or remove opposition access.

commonErrors.error: Team structure collapses around the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain forward, lateral and defensive support.

progressions: Remove the visible clock during play and provide time calls only.
Give teams incomplete information and require leaders to confirm it.
Add interchange or fatigue constraints.
Include scenarios where a behind changes the required result.
Allow the opposition to select the starting tactic.
regressions: Pause play after marks to discuss options.
Use fewer players and a reduced ground.
Provide the preferred tactical response before the repetition.
Increase the scenario time to reduce pressure.
successIndicators: Retain or advance possession according to the scenario.
Protect against turnover in dangerous areas.
Communicate clearly at stoppages and marks.
Execute the required result before time expires.
matchApplication: The final minutes of quarters often produce avoidable scores because players fail to adjust to the scoreboard and clock. This simulation teaches teams to recognise red time and manage possession, territory and risk according to the specific match situation.

title: Late-Score Recovery Simulation
primarySkill: Responding after conceding a late score.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to reset emotionally and tactically after conceding a late score, then execute the correct centre-restart and scoring strategy.
groundSize: Centre square to both goals, using two-thirds to a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two teams.
Set a late-match score and time scenario.
Begin immediately after one team has conceded a goal or behind.
Position players for a centre restart or kick-in according to the score.
Nominate the result required by each team.
Use a visible countdown clock.
Rotate which team is attempting the recovery.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces that one team has just conceded a late score.
Players have 15 seconds to reset, communicate and organise.
Play restarts from the centre or goal square.
The recovering team attempts to generate the required score before time expires.
The opposition attempts to deny possession, control territory and protect the required margin.
Play continues live through all stoppages.
Award the recovering team three points for achieving the required result.
Award the defending team three points for protecting the lead.
After each repetition, players briefly identify the emotional and tactical response.
Change the required score, remaining time and restart type.
coachingPoints: Players must reset immediately rather than discussing the previous score.
Leaders should communicate the required outcome in clear language.
The team must distinguish between needing a goal, any score or simply the next possession.
Centre-restart roles should reflect the required level of risk.
Forwards must create clear scoring lanes and avoid crowding.
Defenders behind the football must anticipate a turnover.
The defending team should use time and territory intelligently.
Emotional urgency must not become rushed execution.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The speed of the team’s emotional reset.
Whether tactical risk matches the required score.
The organisation of midfield and forward structures.
Whether the defending team manages time effectively.

commonErrors.error: Players continue reacting to the conceded score.
commonErrors.correction: Use a reset call and move immediately to the next role.

commonErrors.error: The team attacks without knowing the required result.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm whether a goal, behind or possession is needed.

commonErrors.error: Too many players move forward of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain defensive protection against turnover.

commonErrors.error: The final entry is rushed.
commonErrors.correction: Create one more controlled possession when time permits.

commonErrors.error: The defending team gives the football back quickly.
commonErrors.correction: Retain possession, use the boundary and force the opposition to defend.

progressions: Reduce the time available.
Conceal the exact remaining time and use coach time calls.
Begin with the recovering team outnumbered at the restart.
Add a second scenario immediately after the first.
Allow players to select their own midfield and forward structures.
regressions: Begin with the recovering team in controlled possession.
Pause at the restart to organise roles.
Use non-contact pressure during the first phase.
successIndicators: Communicate the required score and time.
Adjust centre-restart and forward structures appropriately.
matchApplication: Teams frequently concede late scores and then waste the next possession through frustration, poor organisation or excessive urgency. This simulation develops the ability to move immediately from disappointment to purposeful execution.

title: Coach Observation and Feedback Simulation
primarySkill: Observing, reviewing and improving team behaviours during live match simulation.
objective: Develop a repeatable process for coaches and players to observe specific team behaviours, provide concise feedback and apply corrections during the next phase of match simulation.
groundSize: Half to full ground depending on squad size.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two match-simulation teams.
Assign each coach or observer one specific behaviour to monitor.
Observation categories may include stoppage structure, forward pressure, defensive transition, communication, corridor protection or running support.
Prepare three playing blocks of four to six minutes.
Limit feedback between blocks to one or two priority corrections per team.
Nominate player leaders to contribute observations.
Use a scoreboard if competitive intensity is required.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach explains the match scenario and each observer’s focus.
Teams play a live match-simulation block.
Observers record examples rather than general impressions.
At the end of the block, teams separate for a 60- to 90-second review.
Coaches provide one confirmed strength and one priority correction.
Player leaders identify how the correction will be applied.
Teams return immediately for the next block.
Observers check whether the target behaviour improves.
Complete three blocks with the same or progressively adjusted focus.
Finish with a brief comparison between intended and observed behaviours.
coachingPoints: Observation must focus on behaviours that players can change.
Coaches should record specific examples, locations and outcomes.
Feedback must be concise enough to apply immediately.
Avoid correcting every error at once.
Players should explain the tactical meaning of the feedback.
The next block must provide a clear opportunity to apply the correction.
Positive behaviours should be reinforced as specifically as errors are corrected.
Coaches should distinguish skill errors from structural or decision-making errors.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether observers remain focused on their allocated behaviour.
Whether players understand the requested correction.
Whether behaviour changes in the next block.
Whether leaders reinforce the correction during play.
Whether coaching interruptions remain brief and purposeful.

commonErrors.error: Coaches attempt to correct too many issues.
commonErrors.correction: Select the single behaviour with the greatest match impact.

commonErrors.error: Feedback is vague.
commonErrors.correction: Describe the exact moment, location and required alternative.

commonErrors.error: Players listen but cannot explain the correction.
commonErrors.correction: Ask a player leader to restate the action plan.

commonErrors.error: The next block does not test the correction.
commonErrors.correction: Restart from a scenario likely to reproduce the behaviour.

commonErrors.error: Observers watch the football only.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate off-ball structure, communication and transition responsibilities.

progressions: Use video recording for delayed review.
Allow player leaders to deliver the entire feedback break.
Give different observers conflicting priorities and require selection of the main issue.
Track the target behaviour statistically across each block.
Remove coach feedback during the final block.
regressions: Use one team behaviour for all observers.
Pause during play to identify the target behaviour.
Provide observers with a simple checklist.
Reduce player numbers and ground size.
successIndicators: Explain how the correction will be applied.
Demonstrate measurable improvement in the next block.
Maintain match intensity despite review breaks.
matchApplication: Effective match-day coaching depends on recognising the most important issue, communicating it clearly and helping players apply a correction quickly. This simulation develops the observation and feedback process rather than relying only on football execution.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Match-Simulation Fundamentals Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating fundamental match-simulation behaviours across multiple phases of play.
objective: Assess the team’s ability to apply the fundamental match-simulation behaviours developed in MS-001 to MS-009 across connected and changing match scenarios.
groundSize: Two-thirds to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams with normal positional structure.
Prepare five scenario cards covering centre restart, defensive kick-in, boundary stoppage, turnover transition and late-game management.
Assign coaches specific assessment areas.
Use a scoreboard and countdown clock.
Complete five scenario blocks of four to six minutes.
Allow only brief feedback between blocks.
Rotate starting possession and field position.
Record team and individual performance against the success indicators.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach selects and announces the first scenario.
Teams receive 20 seconds to organise before play begins.
Play continues live for the designated block.
Coaches assess structure, decision making, communication, skill execution and turnover reaction.
At the end of the block, teams receive one minute of feedback.
A new scenario begins from a different field position.
At least one block must include a centre restart, one a defensive exit and one a late-score situation.
The final block combines multiple phases without coach direction.
Award points for both scoreboard outcomes and successful tactical behaviours.
Conclude with a player-led review and coach assessment summary.
coachingPoints: Players must identify the match phase and organise without excessive coach direction.
Structures should adapt to field position, score and time.
The first possession in each phase must have a clear purpose.
Teams must maintain balance between attack and defensive protection.
Communication should identify roles, threats and available space.
Turnover reaction must be immediate.
Players should apply previous feedback rather than repeating the same structural error.
Coaches should assess decisions and behaviours, not only the final score.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Centre-restart role clarity and forward connection.
Defensive kick-in spacing and exit selection.
Forward-half pressure and defensive exit balance.
Leadership, communication and response to feedback.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for coaches to organise them.
commonErrors.correction: Require player leaders to establish roles before each restart.

commonErrors.error: Teams use the same tactic in every scenario.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust risk, width and tempo to the score and field position.

commonErrors.error: Strong execution hides poor structure.
commonErrors.correction: Assess whether the method would remain reliable under greater pressure.

commonErrors.error: Players repeat errors identified in previous blocks.
commonErrors.correction: State the correction before the next restart and assign responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Assessment focuses only on goals scored.
commonErrors.correction: Record tactical behaviours, possession quality and turnover response.

progressions: Conduct the final two blocks without announcing the scenario in advance.
Add interchange, fatigue or player-number restrictions.
Use a full match quarter with no coach interruption.
Require players to self-assess before receiving coach feedback.
Record video for detailed review.
regressions: Pause briefly before each restart to organise structure.
Reduce ground size and player numbers.
Provide teams with scenario response cards.
Use controlled contact during early blocks.
successIndicators: Recognise and organise for each match phase.
Execute centre-restart, defensive-exit and stoppage structures.
Select risk according to score, time and field position.
Apply coaching feedback in later blocks.
Create repeatable scoring and defensive outcomes.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the core demands of match simulation into a connected training environment. It allows coaches to determine whether players can transfer isolated tactical concepts into realistic football involving restarts, turnovers, pressure, field position, scoreboard demands and team communication.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation
MS-009 – Coach Observation and Feedback Simulation

title: Defensive-50 Intercept Exit Simulation
primarySkill: Transitioning from a defensive-50 intercept into a controlled exit.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to secure an intercept inside defensive 50, establish composure and exit through the most effective available lane before the opposition can reset its press.
groundSize: Defensive goal line to approximately 20 metres beyond the centre of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team in defensive structure inside and around defensive 50.
Position the opposition in a forward-entry and forward-pressure shape.
Mark a central exit gate and two wide exit gates approximately 15 metres beyond defensive 50.
The coach begins each repetition with a high ball, pressured kick or ground-level entry.
The defensive team attempts to intercept, secure possession and exit.
The attacking team attempts to score or force a repeat entry.
Rotate interceptors, pressure forwards and midfield support players regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach delivers the football into defensive 50 using a nominated entry type.
Defenders compete to mark, spoil or collect the football.
Once possession is secured, the defending team must identify whether to play immediately, hold possession or switch.
The attacking team applies realistic forward pressure.
The defensive team attempts to exit through one of the three gates under control.
Award three points for a central exit, two points for a wide exit and one point for retaining possession for five disposals.
Award the attacking team three points for a goal and two points for a turnover inside 50.
Continue until a score, successful exit, stoppage or football out of bounds.
Reset with a different entry type and starting position.
Rotate team roles after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: The interceptor must complete the mark or gather before searching for an aggressive option.
Nearby defenders should spread immediately to create short and switch options.
Players ahead of the football must work into clear kicking lanes.
The first disposal should reduce pressure and improve the next decision.
The corridor should be used when clearly available rather than forced.
Defenders must communicate pressure from behind.
Ground-level support is required beneath aerial exit targets.
At least one player must remain positioned to defend a turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders are positioned to intercept before the entry.
The quality of the first possession after the turnover.
How quickly teammates create width and depth.
Whether the ball carrier scans both sides of the ground.
Defensive reaction if the exit possession is lost.

commonErrors.error: The interceptor plays on before confirming possession.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the football, balance and then assess the exit.

commonErrors.error: All defenders remain close to the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Spread immediately into short, lateral and long options.

commonErrors.error: The team forces a corridor kick under pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use the wide release or switch when central access is closed.

commonErrors.error: Long exit targets are unsupported.
commonErrors.correction: Place ground-level players front and square of the contest.

commonErrors.error: Players switch off after the first disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue running until the football has fully exited defensive 50.

progressions: Allow the attacking team to set different pressing structures.
Continue play to the opposite goal after a successful exit.
Introduce a six-second limit for the first disposal.
Begin with the defensive team temporarily outnumbered.
Add a late-game scenario requiring either possession or rapid attack.
regressions: Begin with an uncontested intercept mark.
Remove one or two opposition pressure players.
Increase the width of the exit gates.
Allow the coach to nominate the preferred first option.
successIndicators: Spread immediately into useful exit positions.
Select an appropriate central, wide or switch option.
matchApplication: This drill replicates the moment after an intercept mark, spoil or ground-ball win inside defensive 50. It trains defenders to move from emergency defence into composed ball movement while the opposition attempts to maintain forward-half pressure.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Kick-Mark Possession Control Simulation
primarySkill: Controlling match tempo through disciplined kick-mark possession.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to retain possession through purposeful kick-mark football while continuing to improve field position and protect against turnover.
groundSize: Approximately two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide players into two teams across two-thirds of the ground.
Mark three longitudinal lanes: left, corridor and right.
One team begins in possession from half-back.
The possession team attempts to retain the football and advance to a target zone inside 50.
The defending team applies controlled pressure and may intercept.
The possession team must maintain at least one option behind the football.
Rotate starting possession every four minutes.
howTheDrillWorks:
The possession team begins with a mark at half-back.
Players create short, medium and long kicking options.
The team attempts to advance through marks while avoiding unnecessary contests.
Players may use backward or lateral kicks when they create a better forward option.
The defending team attempts to deny the next mark and force a turnover.
Award one point for every five consecutive marks.
Award two points for switching the football and then advancing through the opposite side.
Award three points for a controlled mark inside the attacking target zone.
Award the defending team two points for an intercept and three points if it converts the turnover into a score.
Reset after a score, turnover or football out of bounds.
coachingPoints: The player with the football must scan before and after taking the mark.
Receivers should lead at angles that open the next disposal.
Players must avoid standing directly behind an opponent.
Backward possession is useful only when it changes angle or creates space.
The far side of the ground must remain occupied.
Players behind the football should provide both support and turnover protection.
Kicks should favour the receiver’s safe side.
Tempo should change when the opposition press becomes disorganised.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players lead into clear kicking lanes.
The speed and quality of decisions after marks.
Whether switches improve the team’s next possession.
The positioning of players behind the football.
Kicking placement to the receiver’s advantage.
Whether players recognise when to increase tempo.

commonErrors.error: Players lead directly toward the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Lead on angles that open the next disposal.

commonErrors.error: The team kicks backward without changing the defence.
commonErrors.correction: Use backward possession to access the opposite side or a better angle.

commonErrors.error: The far side becomes empty.
commonErrors.correction: Hold at least one wide option away from the football.

commonErrors.error: Ball movement becomes too slow.
commonErrors.correction: Play on or move quickly when the defence loses shape.

commonErrors.error: All support moves ahead of possession.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain connected options behind and lateral to the ball carrier.

progressions: Reduce the time allowed after each mark.
Permit full defensive pressure after the fifth consecutive mark.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios requiring possession retention.
Require the team to use all three lanes before entering inside 50.
Continue play live after the first turnover.
regressions: Allow one uncontested switch per possession chain.
Pause after each mark to coach leading patterns.
successIndicators: Use the full width of the ground.
Improve angle and field position through each possession.
Maintain defensive protection behind the football.
matchApplication: Teams use kick-mark possession to manage tempo, move an opposition zone, protect a lead or establish a controlled forward entry. This simulation ensures possession remains purposeful rather than becoming slow, predictable ball movement.

title: Corridor Access and Release Simulation
primarySkill: Recognising and using safe corridor access during ball movement.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to identify when the corridor is available, enter it with controlled possession and release the football before opposition pressure closes the space.
groundSize: From defensive 50 to attacking 50 across approximately two-thirds of a ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a corridor approximately 25–30 metres wide through the centre of the ground.
Mark wide release lanes on both sides.
Position one team in possession across half-back and midfield.
Position the opposition in a realistic zone or press.
The possession team scores by entering the corridor and then releasing to an attacking target.
The defending team scores by intercepting inside the corridor.
Rotate starting side and defensive structure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The possession team begins from half-back.
Players move the football until a safe corridor option appears.
A corridor entry must be received under control rather than kicked blindly into space.
Once the corridor is entered, the receiver has a maximum of four seconds to release the football.
The next disposal may continue centrally or move into a wide attacking lane.
Award three points for a corridor entry followed by a controlled inside-50 mark.
Award two points for entering and exiting the corridor without turnover.
Award the defending team three points for an intercept inside the corridor.
Continue play live after turnovers.
Reset after a score, defensive exit or stoppage.
coachingPoints: The corridor should be entered through a clear receiver, not hope.
Players must create the corridor option by moving the opposition first.
The receiver should know the next disposal before receiving.
Support must arrive forward, lateral and behind.
Players should release quickly before the defence collapses.
Wide players must remain available if the corridor closes.
The team must maintain defensive coverage behind the entry.
Communication should identify central access before the ball carrier looks up.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the corridor option is genuinely open.
The receiver’s body position before possession.
The speed of the next disposal.
Supporting movement around the corridor receiver.
The team’s reaction after a central turnover.

commonErrors.error: Players force the corridor because it scores more points.
commonErrors.correction: Enter only when the receiver has space and a next option.

commonErrors.error: The corridor receiver faces backward.
commonErrors.correction: Arrive side-on and scan before receiving.

commonErrors.error: Support players crowd the central space.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain separate lanes and stagger depth.

commonErrors.error: Wide players collapse toward the football.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width as the release option if central play closes.

commonErrors.error: No protection remains behind the football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep connected defenders or midfielders on the defensive side.

progressions: Change the defending team between zone and man-on-man.
Reduce the corridor receiver’s disposal time.
Require the final entry to produce a shot.
Introduce scoreboard consequences for corridor turnovers.
Begin with the possession team under immediate pressure.
regressions: Use passive defenders during the initial ball movement.
Allow the receiver six seconds to release.
successIndicators: Create rather than force corridor access.
Enter through a clearly available receiver.
Release the football before pressure closes.
Connect the corridor entry to an effective forward movement.
matchApplication: Corridor use can produce rapid scoring opportunities but also exposes a team to dangerous turnovers. This simulation develops the judgement, spacing and support required to use central space at the correct moment.

title: Wing Contest and Secondary Possession Simulation
primarySkill: Winning the secondary possession after a long kick to the wing.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to organise around a long wing contest, compete effectively in the air and secure the ground-level possession that follows.
groundSize: A wing channel approximately 70–90 metres long and 40–50 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a long wing channel with boundary and inside edges.
Position one marking target and one aerial defender at the central contest point.
Place three to five ground-level players from each team around the contest.
Position one defensive-cover player behind each team.
The coach or designated kicker begins from half-back.
Mark a forward territory gate 20–25 metres beyond the contest.
Rotate aerial and ground-level roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker delivers a long football toward the wing contest.
The aerial players compete to mark or bring the football to ground.
Ground-level players position for front-and-centre, back, inside and boundary-side outcomes.
The team winning the secondary possession attempts to cross the forward territory gate.
The opposition attempts to force a stoppage, turnover or counterattack.
Award three points for a mark followed by controlled forward possession.
Award two points for winning the ground ball and crossing the territory gate.
Award one point for forcing a forward stoppage.
Continue play through one additional disposal or stoppage.
Reset with a different kick trajectory and contest location.
coachingPoints: The aerial target should compete to mark or direct the football predictably.
Ground-level players must not all stand in front of the contest.
At least one player should protect the inside corridor.
Players should read the flight of the football early.
The first ground-level possession should be protected before disposal.
Support must arrive from both the front and defensive side.
Players should recognise when a stoppage is a successful result.
Defensive-cover players must remain connected to the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The aerial players’ approach and body position.
Distribution of ground-level players around the contest.
Whether the inside corridor is protected.
The quality of the first possession after the spill.

commonErrors.error: All ground-level players position front and centre.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate front, back, inside and defensive-side roles.

commonErrors.error: The aerial target attempts an unrealistic mark.
commonErrors.correction: Compete to bring the football to a predictable area when the mark is unavailable.

commonErrors.error: Players watch the contest rather than moving.
commonErrors.correction: Read the flight early and adjust before the football arrives.

commonErrors.error: The ball winner disposes while unbalanced.
commonErrors.correction: Protect possession, regain feet and then release.

commonErrors.error: No player protects behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold one connected defensive-cover player.

progressions: Add a second aerial player from each team.
Allow full transition to goal after winning possession.
Change the kick between high, flat and boundary-side entries.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios where territory or possession has different value.
Begin with uneven ground-level numbers.
regressions: Use a controlled kick to a nominated contest point.
Reduce contact in the aerial contest.
Stop after the spill to coach positioning.
successIndicators: Organise balanced numbers around the contest.
Secure or neutralise the secondary possession.
Gain territory without exposing a counterattack.
matchApplication: Long kicks to the wing are common during defensive exits and territory battles. The result is often decided by the players positioned around the aerial contest rather than the mark itself.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Forward-Entry Choice Simulation
primarySkill: Selecting the most effective forward-entry option according to pressure and forward positioning.
objective: Develop the connection between ball carriers and forwards so that inside-50 entries match the available space, defensive pressure and scoring opportunity.
groundSize: From approximately 70 metres from goal to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position midfield ball carriers approximately 60–70 metres from goal.
Position forwards and defenders inside 50.
Mark three entry areas: leading lane, deep contest zone and lateral release area.
Place one or two opposition midfield pressure players behind the ball carrier.
Begin each repetition with a handball receive, ground-ball win or mark.
The attacking team attempts to generate a high-quality shot.
Rotate ball carriers, forwards and defenders.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach releases the football to an attacking midfielder.
Forwards create coordinated leading, holding and deep options.
The ball carrier scans the forward structure while managing pressure.
The entry may target a lead, deep contest, lateral option or short possession.
Play continues until a score, defensive rebound or stoppage.
Award three points for a goal.
Award two points for a mark inside 30 metres.
Award one point for a forward entry that creates a controlled ground-ball opportunity.
Award the defending team two points for intercepting and exiting defensive 50.
Reset with a different starting pressure and forward pattern.
coachingPoints: The ball carrier must scan before receiving whenever possible.
Forwards should create separate options at different depths.
Leading players must avoid dragging defenders into a teammate’s space.
The entry should favour the forward’s advantage side.
Deep entries require organised ground-level support.
Players must recognise when no immediate entry is available.
The team should retain possession rather than kick to an outnumbered contest.
Midfielders must protect against a rebound if the entry fails.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The ball carrier’s scanning before and after possession.
Whether the chosen entry matches the available space.

commonErrors.error: Multiple forwards lead into the same lane.
commonErrors.correction: Assign separate depths and entry channels.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier kicks immediately without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Scan before receiving and take one balancing step when time permits.

commonErrors.error: Deep entries have no ground-level support.
commonErrors.correction: Position small forwards front and square before the kick.

commonErrors.error: Players force an entry against an outnumber.
commonErrors.correction: Retain possession and allow the forward structure to reset.

commonErrors.error: The kick is directed to the defender’s side.
commonErrors.correction: Place the football to the forward’s space or protected side.

progressions: Increase pressure on the ball carrier.
Allow defenders to change between man-on-man and zone.
Add a time limit for producing a shot.
Continue play to the opposite goal after a defensive rebound.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios requiring a goal or any score.
regressions: Begin with the ball carrier unpressured.
Increase the size of entry zones.
successIndicators: Create separate leading and deep options.
Match the entry to the available space.
Retain possession when no effective entry exists.
matchApplication: Inside-50 efficiency depends on the relationship between the ball carrier’s decision and the forwards’ movement. This simulation develops purposeful forward entries rather than measuring success only by the number of entries.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation
MS-013 – Corridor Access and Release Simulation

title: Defensive-50 Emergency Response Simulation
primarySkill: Defending an immediate scoring threat inside defensive 50.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to respond collectively when the opposition gains dangerous possession inside defensive 50 and prevent or reduce the quality of the scoring opportunity.
groundSize: Inside defensive 50, including the goal square and pockets.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position attackers and defenders inside 50.
Begin each repetition with the attacking team receiving possession in a dangerous area.
Vary starts between central possession, pocket possession, loose ground ball and marking contest.
Position one or two recovering defenders outside the initial play.
The attackers attempt to score within 15 seconds.
The defenders attempt to prevent a score and exit defensive 50.
Rotate roles after four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach starts play by releasing the football to an attacker or creating a live contest.
Defenders immediately organise goal-side pressure and protect the most dangerous space.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders cover central targets, dangerous receivers and the goal square.
Recovering defenders enter after two to four seconds.
If defenders win possession, they attempt to exit through a marked gate.
Award the attacking team three points for a goal and one point for a behind.
Award the defending team three points for a no-score exit and two points for forcing a low-percentage shot.
Stop after a score, exit or 20 seconds.
Reset from a different dangerous starting position.
coachingPoints: Defenders must protect the goal side before attacking the football.
The nearest defender pressures while teammates cover the next most dangerous options.
Communication should identify free attackers and central threats.
Spoils should be directed away from the corridor where possible.
Ground-level defenders must anticipate the drop zone.
Players should avoid giving away unnecessary free kicks.
After winning possession, the first exit should be safe and supported.
Recovering defenders must run to influence the next action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Communication between pressure and cover defenders.
Protection of the central scoring area.
Direction of spoils and ground-ball support.
Quality of the first exit possession.

commonErrors.error: All defenders attack the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: One pressures while others protect the next dangerous options.

commonErrors.error: Defenders lose goal-side position.
commonErrors.correction: Establish body position between opponent and goal before engaging.

commonErrors.error: Spoils return to the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football toward the boundary or a supported area.

commonErrors.error: Recovering defenders chase from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Recover to the goal square, corridor or free attacker.

commonErrors.error: The exit disposal is rushed.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and use the nearest supported option.

progressions: Begin with the defending team outnumbered.
Allow attackers to retain possession and reset for a second attempt.
Continue full transition after the defensive exit.
Add scoreboard scenarios where conceding a behind is acceptable or unacceptable.
Introduce match-like fatigue before each repetition.
regressions: Begin with equal numbers and known starting positions.
Pause after the start to coach defensive roles.
successIndicators: Apply pressure without losing defensive shape.
matchApplication: Defensive structures are regularly broken by turnovers, missed contests or quick opposition movement. This simulation trains players to survive dangerous moments through collective positioning, communication and composure.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Stoppage-to-Score Chain Simulation
primarySkill: Connecting a stoppage win to a complete scoring chain.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to convert a stoppage win into a connected scoring opportunity through coordinated first possession, support running and forward movement.
groundSize: From a midfield stoppage to the attacking goal.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Establish a stoppage approximately 60–80 metres from goal.
Position rucks, inside midfielders, wings, half-forwards, forwards and defenders.
The coach begins with a ball-up or boundary throw-in.
The team winning possession attacks the goal.
The opposition may counterattack through marked exit gates if it wins the football.
Rotate stoppage combinations and forward structures.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach restarts play from the nominated stoppage.
Both teams compete for first possession.
The winning team attempts to connect the clearance to an outside receiver or controlled territory gain.
Half-forwards and forwards organise according to the direction and speed of the clearance.
Play continues until a score, defensive exit, stoppage or turnover.
Award four points for a goal directly linked to the stoppage win.
Award two points for a controlled inside-50 mark.
Award one point for a forward-half stoppage or repeat entry.
Award the defending team three points for winning possession and exiting through a gate.
Reset with a new stoppage location and tactical plan.
coachingPoints: Stoppage players must understand the intended hit zone and exit route.
The first possession should create a usable second possession.
Outside players must hold their shape until the clearance direction is clear.
Half-forwards should connect the stoppage to the deeper forwards.
Forward movement must respond to the ball carrier’s time and angle.
Players behind the clearance must defend against turnover.
Territory is acceptable when clean possession is unavailable.
Communication should continue from the stoppage through the forward entry.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Quality of the first and second possessions.
Defensive response after a lost clearance.

commonErrors.error: The clearance is hacked forward without support.
commonErrors.correction: Create a receiver or controlled territory outcome before the restart.

commonErrors.error: Wings collapse into the stoppage too early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the football exits.

commonErrors.error: Half-forwards remain too deep.
commonErrors.correction: Provide a connection option between midfield and the deepest forwards.

commonErrors.error: Forwards lead before the ball carrier has control.
commonErrors.correction: Time movement to the quality of the clearance.

commonErrors.error: Players behind the stoppage stop defending.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain turnover protection throughout the attacking chain.

progressions: Change between centre, boundary and around-the-ground stoppages.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Continue full-ground play after a defensive turnover.
Allow teams to nominate and disguise their stoppage plans.
Introduce uneven numbers around the stoppage.
regressions: Begin with a predetermined clearance direction.
Pause after the first possession to coach support positioning.
successIndicators: Connect the first possession to an effective second possession.
Generate a shot or repeat forward-half possession.
matchApplication: Winning a clearance has limited value unless it connects to the next line and produces territory or a scoring opportunity. This drill assesses the complete chain from stoppage structure to forward conversion.

title: Turnover Chain Reaction Simulation
primarySkill: Reacting collectively through multiple changes of possession.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to change roles immediately after each turnover and maintain effective structure through repeated possession changes.
groundSize: Approximately two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams across two-thirds of a ground.
Mark scoring zones at each end.
Begin with one team in possession at half-back.
Allow live play with no stoppage after turnovers unless the football leaves the area.
Position spare footballs with coaches for rapid restart.
Use playing blocks of three to four minutes.
Rotate starting possession between blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in possession and attacks its scoring end.
If possession changes, both teams must immediately reverse attacking and defensive roles.
Play continues through repeated turnovers.
The team gaining possession attempts to use the first three seconds before the opposition resets.
The team losing possession applies pressure and protects dangerous space.
Award three points for a goal and two points for a controlled entry into the scoring zone.
Award one bonus point when a team scores within 12 seconds of a turnover.
Award one defensive point for forcing the opposition backward after losing possession.
Continue for the full playing block.
Review transition behaviour briefly before the next block.
coachingPoints: Players must react to the possession change rather than the outcome of the previous action.
The nearest player pressures immediately after a turnover.
Other defenders protect the corridor and dangerous forward options.
Players gaining possession should spread and accelerate into open space.
Support should exist ahead, lateral and behind the football.
Communication must identify the turnover and new roles.
Players should avoid all running directly toward the football.
Structure must be restored even during repeated chaotic possessions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Immediate pressure on the new ball carrier.
Attacking spread after possession is won.
Ability to restore structure after repeated turnovers.

commonErrors.error: Players pause after making an error.
commonErrors.correction: React to the next possession immediately.

commonErrors.error: Everyone chases the new ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Nearest pressures while others protect space and opponents.

commonErrors.error: The team gaining possession remains compressed.
commonErrors.correction: Spread rapidly into separate attacking lanes.

commonErrors.error: Players communicate too late.
commonErrors.correction: Call “turnover” and identify roles as soon as possession changes.

commonErrors.error: Structure disappears after several turnovers.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish corridor, width and defensive cover on every change.

progressions: Increase the ground size and player numbers.
Add a second football restart immediately after a score.
Introduce a bonus for three consecutive successful transition reactions.
Restrict coach communication during play.
Add late-game score and time pressure.
regressions: Stop after each turnover to organise roles.
Reduce player numbers and ground size.
Nominate the first defensive pressure player.
Limit play to one turnover before resetting.
successIndicators: Apply pressure within seconds of losing possession.
Protect the corridor and goal side.
Restore team structure during chaotic play.
matchApplication: Modern Australian football frequently involves several turnovers within one passage. Teams that respond fastest gain an advantage before formal structures can be restored.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Umpire-Restart Variability Simulation
primarySkill: Organising quickly for unpredictable match restarts.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to recognise different umpire restarts, organise appropriate structures quickly and execute the next phase without relying on extended coach instruction.
groundSize: Half to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two teams with positional structures.
Prepare restart cards including centre bounce, boundary throw-in, ball-up, kick-in, free kick, mark and out-on-the-full.
Establish multiple restart locations across the ground.
The coach or umpire selects restart types without advance warning.
Teams must organise within the normal time available in a match.
Use a scoreboard to create tactical consequences.
Rotate player leadership responsibility.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces or signals a restart type and location.
Players move immediately into the appropriate structure.
The football is restarted using realistic umpire timing.
Play continues live for 30–60 seconds.
Coaches assess organisation, communication and first-phase execution.
Stop play and immediately select a new restart in another area.
Award two points for correct organisation and two points for winning the next phase.
Deduct one point for an unmarked dangerous opponent or incorrect positional setup.
Complete eight to twelve varied restarts.
Finish with two unannounced restarts managed entirely by player leaders.
coachingPoints: Players must recognise the restart before looking to the coach.
Leaders should communicate match-ups, numbers and dangerous space.
Different restart types require different spacing and role priorities.
Players should organise while moving rather than gathering for discussion.
Defensive-side protection remains essential at stoppages.
Free kicks and marks require immediate offensive spread and defensive guarding.
Players must anticipate the likely next phase.
Communication should be brief, clear and role-specific.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players require unnecessary coach direction.

commonErrors.error: Players look to the coach before organising.
commonErrors.correction: Use player leaders to call the structure immediately.

commonErrors.error: Teams use the same setup for every stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust spacing and roles to the restart type and field position.

commonErrors.error: Match-ups are allocated too late.
commonErrors.correction: Identify dangerous opponents while moving into position.

commonErrors.error: Players gather around the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain required width, depth and defensive-side roles.

commonErrors.error: The team organises the restart but not the next phase.
commonErrors.correction: Anticipate where the first possession is likely to travel.

progressions: Reduce communication from coaches and umpires.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios to each restart.
Use deliberate umpire delays or quick restarts.
Include temporary player-number imbalances.
Continue play for longer after each restart.
regressions: Announce the restart type before players move.
Pause to correct structure before releasing the football.
