commonErrors.correction: Hold width until involvement is required.

commonErrors.error: Players remain in contested mode after possession is won.
commonErrors.correction: Spread and transition immediately once the football exits.

progressions: Add scoreboard scenarios following each centre restart.
Allow the clearance to continue to a full scoring outcome.
Begin with one team outnumbered inside the centre square.
Require midfielders to change roles between repetitions.
Introduce repeated centre bounces with limited recovery.
regressions: Use controlled ruck hits to varied but nominated zones.
Reduce contact around the ground ball.
Pause after the ruck contest to identify roles.
Shorten the distance to the scoring gates.
successIndicators: Respond quickly to imperfect ruck outcomes.
Maintain distinct contest and support roles.
Create a usable release after winning possession.
Transition effectively from contest to attack or defence.
matchApplication: Centre bounces often produce deflections, missed hits and secondary contests rather than clean clearances. This simulation develops the recovery organisation required when the planned stoppage outcome breaks down.
relatedDrills: MS-033 – Congestion Escape Handball Chain Simulation

title: Pressured Defensive Exit Chain Simulation
primarySkill: Maintaining possession through multiple pressured disposals while exiting defensive 50.
objective: Develop the defensive group’s ability to complete a connected exit chain under sustained forward pressure without transferring greater pressure to the next receiver.
groundSize: Defensive goal line to approximately 25 metres beyond defensive 50.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position defenders inside defensive 50.
Organise opposition forwards in a connected press.
Mark central and wide exit gates beyond defensive 50.
Begin each repetition with a defender winning possession under immediate pressure.
Require the defensive team to complete at least three connected possessions before exiting.
Position support players at varied depths.
Rotate initial ball winners and pressure players.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach delivers a contested football to a defender.
The defender secures possession while an opponent applies immediate pressure.
Teammates create forward, lateral and behind-support options.
The defensive team must complete at least three disposals before crossing an exit gate.
The pressing team maintains live pressure and attempts to force a turnover.
Players may kick, handball, switch or carry according to the available space.
Award three points for exiting through the corridor after three or more possessions.
Award two points for a controlled wide exit.
Award the pressing team three points for a turnover and goal.
Reset after an exit, score, stoppage or 30 seconds.
coachingPoints: The first ball winner must secure possession before looking to release.
Each disposal should reduce pressure or improve the next player’s angle.
Receivers must move before the previous disposal is completed.
Behind-support should remain available when forward options close.
Players should not handball to stationary teammates surrounded by pressure.
The far side must remain available for a switch.
The team should accelerate once the press is broken.
Turnover protection remains necessary throughout the exit chain.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether each disposal improves the team’s situation.
Availability of behind and far-side support.
Decision to kick, handball, carry or switch.

commonErrors.error: The first defender disposes while off balance.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the football, regain balance and then release.

commonErrors.error: Players handball to a teammate under greater pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Select a receiver with time, space or a better angle.

commonErrors.error: Support players wait until the ball carrier looks at them.
commonErrors.correction: Move early and communicate before the disposal.

commonErrors.error: All options move forward of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a behind-support outlet.

commonErrors.error: Players slow down after breaking the first pressure line.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate before the opposition press can recover.

progressions: Increase the number of opposition pressure players.
Reduce the available exit width.
Require a full-ground scoring chain after the exit.
Introduce a decision clock for each possession.
Start with the defensive team outnumbered.
regressions: Reduce the pressing team by one or two players.
Allow the first possession to be uncontested.
Increase the width of the exit gates.
Pause after each possession to coach support movement.
successIndicators: Recognise when the press has been broken.
matchApplication: Defensive exits rarely occur through one uncontested disposal. This simulation develops the composure and support required to survive several pressure actions before the team reaches open space.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Forward-Half Repeat Contest Simulation
primarySkill: Maintaining attacking pressure through repeated forward-half contests.
objective: Develop the attacking team’s ability to remain connected through repeated contests, recover loose footballs and create additional scoring opportunities without losing forward-half structure.
groundSize: Attacking half of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team in forward-half attacking structure.
Position the opposition in defensive-50 exit structure.
Start with a pressured forward entry or aerial contest.
Place midfield and high-forward players outside the immediate contest.
The attacking team attempts to generate repeat contests and scoring opportunities.
The defending team attempts to secure possession and exit beyond the centre line.
Rotate attacking and defending roles after four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a contested forward entry.
Players compete for the mark, spoil or ground-level possession.
If the attacking team retains or regains the football, play continues immediately.
High forwards and midfielders position for repeat entries and defensive coverage.
The defending team attempts to exit through central or wide gates.
Award the attacking team three points for a goal.
Award two points for a turnover won inside 50.
Award one point for generating a repeat inside-50 entry.
Award the defending team three points for a controlled exit beyond the centre line.
Stop after a score, successful exit or 60 seconds.
coachingPoints: Players must expect the first forward entry not to produce a clean mark.
Ground-level positioning should cover front, back and dangerous central areas.
The nearest player applies pressure while others maintain the lock-in shape.
High forwards should remain connected to the contest without crowding it.
Midfielders must position to intercept defensive exits.
Players should direct spills toward teammates where possible.
The attacking team must react immediately after a defensive mark or gather.
Pressure must remain legal and controlled.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ground-level positioning around the first contest.
Work rate after the opposition gains possession.

commonErrors.error: Players assume the first entry will be marked.
commonErrors.correction: Organise front, back and ground-level support before the ball arrives.

commonErrors.error: Multiple forwards chase the same defender.
commonErrors.correction: One pressures while others close the next exits.

commonErrors.error: High forwards move too close to the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold connection space outside the immediate congestion.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders stand too deep to create a repeat entry.
commonErrors.correction: Move close enough to intercept or receive the rebound.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after a defensive mark.
commonErrors.correction: Set the mark, guard the corridor and prepare for the next disposal.

progressions: Begin with lower-quality forward entries.
Allow the defending team to launch a full counterattack.
Add repeated footballs without a complete reset.
Introduce scoreboard conditions rewarding repeat entries.
Reduce recovery time between repetitions.
regressions: Begin with the attacking team having an extra forward.
Use controlled rather than full contact.
Restrict defensive exits to wide gates.
Pause after the first contest to coach positioning.
successIndicators: Prepare for the second and third contests.
Continue working after the opposition gains possession.
matchApplication: Forward-half pressure depends on the team’s ability to survive multiple contests rather than expecting each entry to create an immediate score. This simulation develops repeat effort, positioning and lock-in structure.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation
MS-014 – Wing Contest and Secondary Possession Simulation
MS-042 – Pressured Defensive Exit Chain Simulation

title: Outnumbered Defence Delay Simulation
primarySkill: Delaying an opposition attack while temporarily outnumbered.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to protect the most dangerous space, delay the ball carrier and allow teammates time to recover when the opposition has a numerical advantage.
groundSize: A transition area 70–100 metres long and 45–60 metres wide leading toward goal.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Arrange attacking groups with a numerical advantage such as five against three or six against four.
Position defenders between the attackers and goal.
Place recovering defenders behind the play.
Mark a central scoring corridor and two wider lanes.
Begin each repetition with a turnover or clean attacking possession.
Recovering defenders enter after four to six seconds.
Rotate initial and recovering defensive roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession and advances toward goal.
Initial defenders organise to protect the corridor and deepest scoring threat.
The nearest defender pressures only when support and cover are established.
Other defenders guard space and likely receivers.
Recovering defenders sprint into useful positions.
The attack continues until a score, turnover or defensive recovery.
Award the attacking team three points for a goal before numbers become equal.
Award the defending team two points for delaying until recovery arrives.
Award three defensive points for forcing a turnover or low-percentage shot.
Reset with a different numerical advantage.
coachingPoints: Outnumbered defenders must protect space before chasing opponents.
The corridor and goal-side position take priority.
Pressure should be applied when it forces the attack away from danger.
Defenders should communicate which opponent or space each player controls.
The deepest defender organises the line.
Recovering players should run to the next dangerous position.
Defenders should avoid committing two players to the ball carrier.
Once equal numbers are restored, defenders may become more aggressive.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Protection of central and goal-side space.
Timing of pressure on the ball carrier.
Change from delay to active defence when numbers recover.

commonErrors.error: The nearest defender charges the ball carrier immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Delay until pressure can force play away from danger.

commonErrors.error: Defenders each follow an opponent and expose the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Protect central space and hand over low-threat options.

commonErrors.error: Two defenders commit to the same attacker.
commonErrors.correction: One pressures while the other covers the next possession.

commonErrors.error: Recovering players chase directly behind opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Sprint to goal-side or the next dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Defenders remain passive after numbers recover.
commonErrors.correction: Increase pressure once cover and equal numbers are established.

progressions: Increase the attacking advantage.
Shorten the distance to goal.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
Allow full contact.
Continue play after a defensive turnover.
regressions: Pause after the first possession to organise roles.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor and goal side.
Allow recovering teammates to influence play.
matchApplication: Teams are often temporarily outnumbered after turnovers, missed tackles or broken structures. This simulation teaches defenders to survive the vulnerable period until support arrives.

title: Numbers-at-Contest Release Simulation
primarySkill: Using numerical support around a contest to create a clean possession release.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to bring appropriate numbers to a contest, maintain distinct roles and release the football to an outside player without overcrowding the ball.
groundSize: A contested area 25 x 25 metres connected to a 50–70-metre transition zone.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central contest zone.
Position three to five players from each team inside or around the zone.
Position outside runners in separate exit lanes.
Begin with a ground ball, high ball or tackled-player release.
The team winning possession attempts to use its numerical support to release an outside runner.
The opposition attempts to trap the football or win possession.
Rotate inside, support and outside roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach starts a live contested football.
The nearest players compete for possession.
Supporting players establish ball-winner, protector, receiver and outside-release roles.
The team winning the football attempts to move it outside the contest.
Players may use handball, shepherding, blocking within the laws or a short kick.
The outside receiver attacks through an exit gate or toward goal.
Award three points for a clean release followed by controlled transition.
Award two points for a release created by a legal shepherd or block.
Award the defending team three points for trapping the football or winning turnover.
Reset with a different contest type.
coachingPoints: Bringing numbers to the contest does not mean every player attacks the football.
One player wins or protects the football.
Supporting players create separation and clear release angles.
Outside runners should remain outside the congestion.
Legal shepherds and blocks should protect the release without holding.
The receiver must communicate before the ball winner gains control.
If the opposition wins possession, outside players must close space immediately.
Players should accept a stoppage when no safe release exists.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Quality of protection around the ball winner.

commonErrors.error: Every player attacks the football.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate ball-winner, protector, receiver and outside roles.

commonErrors.error: Outside runners enter congestion too early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the release is ready.

commonErrors.error: Support players stand too close to the ball winner.
commonErrors.correction: Create usable angles and separation.

commonErrors.error: Players block illegally or hold opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Use body position and legal shepherding only.

commonErrors.error: The team forces a release into pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the football and create a stoppage when necessary.

progressions: Increase contact and pressure.
Reduce the size of the contest zone.
Add recovering defenders to the transition area.
Continue play to a full scoring outcome.
Begin with the possession team outnumbered.
regressions: Increase the size of the contest area.
Pause after possession is secured to assign roles.
successIndicators: Bring useful rather than excessive numbers.
Maintain clear contest and support roles.
matchApplication: Winning contested possession requires more than numbers around the football. This simulation develops the role clarity needed to turn numerical support into a clean attacking release.
relatedDrills: MS-033 – Congestion Escape Handball Chain Simulation

title: Aerial Spill Recovery Simulation
primarySkill: Recovering team possession and structure after an aerial contest spills to ground.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to anticipate an aerial spill, organise players around the drop zone and secure or neutralise the football after the marking contest.
groundSize: A contest area approximately 45 x 45 metres with attacking and defensive exit zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one or two aerial players from each team at a nominated contest point.
Place ground-level players around the likely drop zone.
Mark front, rear, inside and boundary-side reference areas.
Establish attacking and defensive exit gates.
The coach varies the height, depth and direction of the kick.
Players do not know whether the football will be marked or spilled.
Rotate aerial and ground-level roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach delivers a high football to the aerial contest.
Players compete to mark or spoil.
Ground-level players adjust according to the flight and body position of the aerial players.
If the football spills, both teams compete for possession.
The team winning the ground ball attempts to exit through its attacking gate.
The opposition applies immediate pressure and attempts to force a stoppage.
Award three points for securing the spill and completing a controlled exit.
Award two points for directing the spoil to a teammate.
Award one point for neutralising a dangerous opposition recovery.
Reset with a different kick and contest location.
coachingPoints: Ground-level players must read the flight rather than stand at preset cones.
The likely spill changes according to the aerial players’ approach and body position.
Teams should cover front, back and dangerous inside space.
The aerial player should direct the football predictably when a mark is unavailable.
The first ground-level possession must be secured before release.
Players should avoid all standing directly beneath the football.
Defensive coverage must remain behind the contest.
Communication should identify likely spill direction before contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Adjustment to the flight of the football.
Distribution of players around the drop zone.
Security of the first ground-level possession.

commonErrors.error: Ground-level players stand directly under the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Position around the likely spill zones.

commonErrors.error: Players remain fixed despite the football’s changing flight.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust continuously as the ball and aerial players move.

commonErrors.error: The spoil returns to dangerous central space.
commonErrors.correction: Direct it toward the boundary or a supported teammate.

commonErrors.error: The first ground-ball winner disposes immediately under pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Protect possession and identify support first.

commonErrors.error: No player remains behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain defensive cover against a clean opposition win.

progressions: Add a second aerial contest immediately after the first.
Continue transition to goal after the exit.
Use flatter and less predictable kicks.
Introduce uneven ground-level numbers.
Add scoreboard consequences for losing central spills.
regressions: Use controlled kicks to a consistent contest point.
Mark likely spill zones with cones.
Stop after the spill to coach positioning.
successIndicators: Read and adjust to the aerial contest.
Direct or recover the football safely.
Provide support around the ball winner.
Maintain defensive coverage behind the contest.
matchApplication: Many marking contests are decided by players positioned at ground level. This simulation develops the ability to anticipate, recover and transition from aerial spills in realistic match conditions.
relatedDrills: MS-014 – Wing Contest and Secondary Possession Simulation

title: Boundary Pressure Lock Simulation
primarySkill: Using the boundary to trap opposition possession and force a turnover or repeat stoppage.
objective: Develop the defending team’s ability to apply coordinated pressure near the boundary, deny inside release and force the opposition into a turnover, stoppage or backward possession.
groundSize: A boundary channel approximately 70 metres long and 30–40 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a long channel along the boundary.
Position one team in possession near the boundary.
Position the defending team in a pressure structure.
Mark an inside release gate and a forward territory gate.
The possession team attempts to escape through the inside gate or advance through the territory gate.
The defending team attempts to trap possession and force a turnover or stoppage.
Rotate team roles after four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The possession team begins with a mark or ground-ball win near the boundary.
The nearest defender applies pressure from the inside.
Supporting defenders close short, backward and central options.
The boundary acts as an additional defensive barrier.
The possession team attempts to escape or gain territory.
Award the possession team three points for a controlled inside release.
Award two points for crossing the territory gate.
Award the defending team three points for a turnover.
Award two defensive points for forcing a repeat boundary stoppage.
Reset from a different position along the channel.
coachingPoints: The first defender should pressure from the inside and send play toward the boundary.
Supporting defenders must close the next likely release options.
Players should avoid overcommitting and allowing an inside handball.
The team must remain connected behind the pressure.
Boundary-side pressure should be aggressive but legal.
Defenders should recognise when a repeat stoppage is a successful outcome.
If possession is won, the team should spread away from the boundary.
Communication should identify inside receivers and backward exits.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Angle of the first pressure action.
Control of backward and short options.
Ability to force a stoppage or turnover.
Transition movement after possession is won.

commonErrors.error: The first defender pressures from the boundary side.
commonErrors.correction: Approach from inside and force play toward the line.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defenders all chase the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Close the next receivers and maintain connection.

commonErrors.error: Defenders dive into tackles and allow an inside release.
commonErrors.correction: Stay balanced and pressure the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Players consider a stoppage a failed result.
commonErrors.correction: Recognise a trapped boundary stoppage as territorial control.

commonErrors.error: The team remains compressed after winning possession.
commonErrors.correction: Spread immediately to create an exit from the boundary.

progressions: Reduce the width of the boundary channel.
Allow the possession team an extra player.
Continue play after the boundary stoppage.
Add scoreboard scenarios where territory is critical.
Introduce repeated efforts with minimal recovery.
regressions: Pause after the first defensive action to coach positioning.
successIndicators: Force backward possession, stoppage or turnover.
Spread effectively after winning the football.
matchApplication: The boundary can assist team defence when pressure is applied from the correct angle. This simulation develops the ability to trap possession without allowing an easy inside escape.

title: Corridor Turnover Containment Simulation
primarySkill: Containing an opposition attack after losing possession in the corridor.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to respond to a dangerous central turnover by applying immediate pressure, protecting goal-side space and delaying the opposition’s scoring opportunity.
groundSize: A central corridor from defensive 50 to attacking 50 with wider recovery lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor and two outside recovery lanes.
Position one team in attacking possession through the corridor.
Position opposition players to intercept or win a turnover.
Place defenders behind and beside the initial possession.
Begin with a central disposal that may be completed, spoiled or intercepted.
On turnover, the opposition attacks the nearest goal.
Rotate the starting ball carrier and turnover location.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts a central possession.
The coach or opposition creates a turnover at varying points in the corridor.
The nearest former attacker pressures the new ball carrier immediately.
Teammates recover goal side and protect central scoring lanes.
Wide players fold inward to support containment.
The opposition attempts to score before the defensive structure recovers.
Award the attacking turnover team three points for a goal within 12 seconds.
Award the recovering team two points for delaying the attack beyond 12 seconds.
Award three recovery points for forcing a turnover or wide low-percentage entry.
Reset with a different central turnover.
coachingPoints: The nearest player must pressure immediately after the turnover.
Other players should protect goal-side and central space rather than all chasing.
Recovery runs should angle toward the dangerous lane.
Wide players must decide when to fold inward.
Defenders behind the football should delay rather than overcommit.
Communication must identify the most dangerous receiver.
The team should force the opposition toward the boundary.
Once possession is regained, players should exit away from the turnover pressure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Speed of pressure after the turnover.
Ability to regain possession and exit.

commonErrors.error: Players react emotionally to the turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Move immediately to pressure or recovery responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Everyone chases the new ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Nearest pressures while others protect space and receivers.

commonErrors.error: Recovery runs follow opponents from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Angle toward goal-side and central danger.

commonErrors.error: Wide players remain disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Fold inward when the corridor turnover creates immediate threat.

commonErrors.error: Defenders dive in and allow the attack through.
commonErrors.correction: Delay and force play toward a less dangerous lane.

progressions: Create turnovers closer to goal.
Increase the attacking numbers after turnover.
Reduce the recovery time available.
Continue full-ground play after containment.
Add late-match scoreboard consequences.
regressions: Pause immediately after the turnover to organise roles.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor and scoring zone.
Regain possession or force a lower-quality entry.
matchApplication: Central turnovers create some of the most dangerous scoring opportunities in Australian football. This simulation develops the immediate collective response required to limit their damage.
relatedDrills: MS-013 – Corridor Access and Release Simulation

title: Fatigue-Pressure Decision Simulation
primarySkill: Maintaining decision quality and skill execution under accumulated match-like fatigue and pressure.
objective: Develop players’ ability to continue making appropriate tactical decisions and executing fundamental skills after repeated high-intensity efforts.
groundSize: Half to two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Mark scoring zones at each end.
Prepare repeated playing blocks of 90 seconds to two minutes.
Begin each block from a contested restart.
Allow full transition and scoring.
Provide only short recovery between blocks.
Change the tactical objective as fatigue accumulates.
Monitor technique and remove players if fatigue creates unsafe movement.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams begin from a contested restart.
Play continues at match intensity for the allocated block.
Coaches introduce a new tactical condition during play, such as protect the corridor, retain possession or score quickly.
Players must recognise and apply the condition while fatigued.
Natural turnovers and stoppages continue live.
At the end of the block, players receive 30–45 seconds of recovery.
The next block begins from a different restart or field position.
Award points for scores and correct tactical decisions.
Deduct behaviour points for avoidable rushed disposals or structural breakdowns.
Complete four to six blocks according to player level and safety.
coachingPoints: Fatigue does not remove the need to scan before possession.
Players should simplify decisions when execution quality declines.
Communication must increase as physical capacity decreases.
Players should maintain running technique and legal contact.
The first option is not always the safest option.
Teams must preserve structure rather than allowing fatigue to create uncontrolled congestion.
Players should recognise when to retain possession and when to gain territory.
Coaches should prioritise decision quality and safety over exhaustion.

commonErrors.error: Players dispose immediately because they are tired.
commonErrors.correction: Scan and select the safest effective option.

commonErrors.error: Communication decreases as fatigue increases.
commonErrors.correction: Demand earlier and louder role calls.

commonErrors.error: Team structure collapses around the football.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve width, depth and behind support.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt low-percentage skills while off balance.
commonErrors.correction: Simplify the disposal and protect possession.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue produces unsafe tackling or movement.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce intensity, remove the player or finish the repetition.

progressions: Reduce recovery between blocks.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
Increase tactical changes during play.
Introduce temporary numerical imbalances.
Play a final block without coach communication.
regressions: Reduce ground size and player numbers.
matchApplication: Important decisions often occur late in quarters or after repeated high-intensity passages. This simulation tests whether players can preserve tactical discipline and skill execution when physically and mentally fatigued.
relatedDrills: MS-040 – Match-Simulation Movement and Connection Assessment

title: Pressure and Contest Phase Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating pressure, contest and recovery behaviours across connected match phases.
objective: Assess whether the team can independently apply the pressure and contest principles developed in MS-041 to MS-049 during continuous, changing and physically demanding match simulation.
groundSize: Two-thirds to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams with interchange players.
Prepare scenario cards covering centre-bounce recovery, defensive exit, forward-half contest, outnumbered defence, boundary pressure and corridor turnover.
Assign coaches specific pressure and contest behaviours to assess.
Establish a scoreboard and countdown clock.
Play three blocks of eight to ten minutes.
Use short player-led reviews between blocks.
Introduce fatigue through repeated live phases rather than separate running.
Use minimal coach intervention during play.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the first starting scenario.
Teams organise and begin live play.
After the initial scenario, play continues without restrictions.
Coaches assess contest roles, pressure positioning, support, recovery and transition.
Natural stoppages and turnovers remain live.
At the end of each block, teams complete a two-minute player-led review.
The next block begins from a different scenario and scoreboard condition.
Award points for match score and nominated pressure behaviours.
The final block is played under accumulated fatigue with no advance tactical instruction.
Conclude with team and individual assessment against the success indicators.
coachingPoints: Players must maintain distinct roles around contests.
Pressure should direct play rather than simply chase the football.
Defensive-side and goal-side protection remain essential.
Teams should recognise when a stoppage or territory gain is a successful outcome.
The first possession after a contest must be secure.
Players must support both the release and the possible turnover.
Outnumbered defenders should delay until help arrives.
Fatigue must not remove communication or tactical discipline.
Coaches should assess repeatable pressure behaviours rather than isolated effort.
Contact and tackling must remain legal and safe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Numbers and roles around contested possession.

commonErrors.error: Players confuse pressure with chasing the football.
commonErrors.correction: Pressure from angles that protect dangerous space and close the next option.

commonErrors.error: Contest numbers arrive without clear roles.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate ball-winner, protector, receiver and outside support.

commonErrors.error: Players force releases from unsafe situations.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession or accept a stoppage when necessary.

commonErrors.error: Defensive structure collapses after repeated efforts.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish corridor, goal-side and behind-the-ball coverage.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue leads to rushed skills or unsafe contact.
commonErrors.correction: Simplify execution and reduce load when technique breaks down.

progressions: Play a full quarter without coach interruption.
Use hidden scenario objectives for each team.
Reduce interchange availability.
Add final-minute scoreboard pressure.
Record the assessment for detailed review.
regressions: Use four scenarios rather than six.
Provide player leaders with pressure-role reminder cards.
successIndicators: Exit defensive pressure through connected possession.
Bring useful numbers and clear roles to contests.
Use the boundary to trap possession.
matchApplication: This assessment completes the first pressure-and-contest block of the Match Simulation chapter. It determines whether players can apply coordinated pressure, contest roles, recovery structure and decision making under fatigue within continuous Australian football.
relatedDrills: MS-042 – Pressured Defensive Exit Chain Simulation

title: Defensive-50 Siege Reset Simulation
primarySkill: Resetting defensive structure during repeated opposition forward entries.
objective: Develop the defensive unit’s ability to survive repeated forward entries, restore structure after each contest and identify the correct moment to exit rather than returning possession immediately.
groundSize: Defensive 50 extending approximately 20 metres beyond the arc.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position one team in defensive structure inside defensive 50.
Position the opposition with forwards, high forwards and midfielders around the attacking arc.
Place several footballs with coaches outside 50.
Mark central and wide defensive exit gates beyond the arc.
The attacking team receives repeated entries from varying angles.
The defending team must prevent scores, reset after each contest and eventually complete a controlled exit.
Rotate defenders, forwards and midfield support players after each block.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a forward entry from approximately 60 metres.
Defenders compete to mark, spoil or secure the ground ball.
If the defending team does not complete a controlled exit, the coach immediately introduces another football.
The attacking team resets its forward pressure and attempts to create another score.
Defenders must reorganise match-ups, goal-side coverage and ground-level support between entries.
A defensive possession counts as controlled only when the team completes two possessions or crosses an exit gate.
Award the attacking team three points for a goal and two points for a turnover won inside 50.
Award the defending team two points for preventing a score through three consecutive entries.
Award three defensive points for completing a controlled exit.
End the repetition after a successful exit, goal or four consecutive entries.
coachingPoints: Defenders must reset immediately after every spoil, stoppage or rushed disposal.
Goal-side and central protection take priority during repeated entries.
The deepest defender should organise match-ups and dangerous space.
Ground-level players must prepare for spills rather than watch aerial contests.
The first defensive possession must reduce pressure.
Players should avoid clearing directly back to an unopposed opposition player.
Communication must continue despite fatigue and repeated contests.
Once the exit opportunity appears, players should spread decisively.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Quality of the first possession after a regain.
Whether defenders recognise the correct exit moment.

commonErrors.error: Defenders remain focused on the previous contest.
commonErrors.correction: Reset match-ups and dangerous-space responsibilities immediately.

commonErrors.error: Players all collapse to the goal square.
commonErrors.correction: Protect central danger while maintaining coverage of likely receivers.

commonErrors.error: Ground-level defenders watch the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Move early to front, back and dangerous spill locations.

commonErrors.error: Clearances return directly to the opposition.
commonErrors.correction: Use a supported disposal or direct territory toward the boundary.

commonErrors.error: Communication decreases as fatigue builds.
commonErrors.correction: Require the deepest defender and midfield leaders to continue organising.

progressions: Increase the speed and quality of consecutive entries.
Begin with the defending team outnumbered.
Allow the attacking team to change forward structure between entries.
Require the defensive exit to reach the centre line.
Add a late-game scenario where conceding any score loses the repetition.
regressions: Limit the sequence to two forward entries.
Allow the first defensive mark to be uncontested.
Restrict entries to one side of the ground.
Pause briefly between entries to organise defensive roles.
successIndicators: Reset defensive structure after every contest.
Use the first possession to reduce danger.
matchApplication: Teams often face periods of sustained opposition pressure involving repeated entries, stoppages and incomplete clearances. This simulation develops the resilience and organisation required to survive those phases and regain control.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation
MS-050 – Pressure and Contest Phase Assessment

title: High-Ball Defensive Exit Contest Simulation
primarySkill: Exiting defensive territory through a structured high-ball contest.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to organise a long defensive exit, create a competitive aerial contest and control the secondary possession around the target.
groundSize: Defensive goal line to approximately 25 metres beyond the centre.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team in possession inside defensive 50.
Establish a long marking target near the wing or centre.
Position aerial defenders and ground-level players around the target.
Mark front, rear, inside and boundary-side support zones.
Position one defensive-cover player behind the contest.
The exiting team attempts to gain territory or retain possession.
The opposition attempts to intercept and return the football inside 50.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defensive team begins with possession inside 50.
Short options are initially pressured, encouraging consideration of a long exit.
The ball carrier selects a high-ball target.
The aerial players compete to mark, neutralise or direct the football.
Ground-level players contest the secondary possession.
The exiting team attempts to cross a forward territory line.
Award three points for a mark followed by controlled forward possession.
Award two points for winning the spill and crossing the territory line.
Award one point for creating a forward stoppage.
Award the opposition three points for an intercept or clean return entry.
coachingPoints: The long target must provide a genuine contest rather than stand underneath the football.
Ground-level roles should include front, rear, inside and defensive-side coverage.
The kick should favour the target’s protected side.
Players must anticipate the likely spoil direction.
The team should recognise when a forward stoppage is an acceptable result.
Defensive-cover players must remain connected behind the contest.
If the secondary possession is won, players should spread immediately.
The kicker must avoid choosing an isolated target surrounded by opposition numbers.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Selection and positioning of the long target.
Direction of marks, spoils and spills.

commonErrors.error: The target waits flat-footed under the football.
commonErrors.correction: Approach the contest with momentum and strong body position.

commonErrors.error: All ground-level players stand front and centre.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate front, back, inside and defensive-side roles.

commonErrors.error: The kick is placed to the defender’s advantage.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football to the target’s protected side.

commonErrors.error: Players treat a forward stoppage as failure.
commonErrors.correction: Recognise territory and a reset as a positive defensive outcome.

commonErrors.error: No player protects behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a connected defensive-cover player.

progressions: Add a second aerial target and defender.
Allow the opposition to vary its press.
Continue play to the opposite goal after winning the secondary possession.
Begin with the exiting team outnumbered around the contest.
Add a scoreboard scenario requiring possession rather than territory.
regressions: Use a controlled kick to a nominated target area.
Stop after the aerial contest to coach secondary positioning.
successIndicators: Transition quickly after winning the secondary ball.
matchApplication: Teams frequently need to escape defensive pressure through a long kick. Success depends on the organisation around the contest rather than the kick alone.
relatedDrills: MS-014 – Wing Contest and Secondary Possession Simulation
MS-042 – Pressured Defensive Exit Chain Simulation

title: Ground-Level Forward Pressure Wave Simulation
primarySkill: Applying repeated ground-level forward pressure after an imperfect entry.
objective: Develop the forward group’s ability to create consecutive pressure actions after the football reaches ground level and convert opposition uncertainty into a turnover or scoring opportunity.
groundSize: Inside attacking 50.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position attackers and defenders inside 50.
Begin with a low, bouncing or spoiled forward entry.
Position high forwards and midfielders near the attacking arc.
The defenders attempt to secure the football and exit through marked gates.
The forwards attempt to create repeated pressure actions and regain possession.
Limit each repetition to 30–40 seconds.
Rotate forward and defensive roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach introduces an imperfect forward entry.
Players compete for the ground-level possession.
The nearest forward pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting forwards close likely handball, kick and escape options.
If the football is released, the next forward applies pressure immediately.
The attacking team attempts to regain possession and score.
Award three points for a goal following a pressure turnover.
Award two points for forcing a turnover inside 50.
Award one point for forcing a stoppage or rushed disposal.
Award the defending team three points for a controlled exit.
coachingPoints: The nearest forward must close space under control.
Supporting forwards should protect the next disposal rather than all tackling the ball carrier.
Pressure should continue through the second and third possessions.
Players must remain goal side of likely receivers where possible.
Tackles must be legal, safe and completed with strong body position.
High forwards should prevent easy outlet kicks.
Players must react instantly when a teammate is beaten.
After regaining possession, attackers should settle enough to select a quality shot.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Coordination between first and second pressure players.
Repeat effort after an initial missed tackle.
Decision quality after possession is regained.

commonErrors.error: Multiple forwards attack the same ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: One pressures while others close the next options.

commonErrors.error: Players overrun the tackle.
commonErrors.correction: Decelerate, stay balanced and control the ball carrier’s movement.

commonErrors.error: Pressure stops after the first disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Identify and attack the next receiver immediately.

commonErrors.error: High forwards stand too deep to affect the exit.
commonErrors.correction: Position close enough to intercept or pressure the outlet.

commonErrors.error: Players rush the shot after regaining possession.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the football and select the highest-percentage option.

progressions: Increase defensive numbers.
Begin with the forward team outnumbered.
Continue play after a successful defensive exit.
Introduce repeated entries without full recovery.
Add a late-game scenario requiring a goal.
regressions: Begin with controlled rather than full contact.
Limit defenders to handball exits initially.
Increase the size of the pressure area.
Pause after each disposal to identify the next pressure role.
successIndicators: Regain possession or force a stoppage.
Convert pressure wins into quality scoring opportunities.
matchApplication: Forward pressure is most effective when it occurs as a connected wave rather than one isolated tackle attempt. This simulation develops the repeat actions required to keep the football inside attacking 50.
relatedDrills: MS-005 – Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation

title: Midfield Counter-Pressure Compression Simulation
primarySkill: Compressing space immediately after losing possession through the midfield.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to reduce opposition time and space immediately after a midfield turnover while preserving protection against a clean forward release.
groundSize: A midfield area approximately 80 metres long and 60 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor and two wide lanes.
Position both teams across midfield and half-forward.
Begin with one team circulating possession.
The coach creates or calls a turnover at an unpredictable moment.
The team losing possession must compress around the football and protect the next forward option.
The team winning possession attempts to escape the pressure and cross an attacking gate.
Rotate starting possession.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in controlled possession.
The coach creates a turnover through a loose disposal, intercept or contested release.
The nearest former attacker pressures the new ball carrier.
Teammates compress the space around likely receivers.
Players behind the turnover protect the corridor and deepest attacking option.
The team in possession attempts to escape through the corridor or wide gates.
Award three points for escaping pressure and crossing a forward gate.
Award the counter-pressing team three points for regaining possession within eight seconds.
Award two points for forcing a stoppage or backward disposal.
Reset after an escape, regain, stoppage or 20 seconds.
coachingPoints: Counter-pressure begins immediately when possession changes.
The nearest player attacks the ball carrier’s time and space.
Supporting players compress around the next likely disposal.
The team must not abandon protection behind the football.
Players should force the opposition toward lower-value space.
Communication must identify pressure, cover and deepest threat.
The press should expand again once possession is regained.
Players must avoid reckless contact when attempting to win the football back.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Pressure on the new ball carrier.
Communication between pressure and cover players.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after making the turnover error.
commonErrors.correction: React immediately and influence the next possession.

commonErrors.error: Everyone attacks the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: One pressures while others close receivers and protect depth.

commonErrors.error: The team compresses but leaves the corridor exposed.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a connected player protecting central release.

commonErrors.error: Pressure players arrive out of control.
commonErrors.correction: Close space quickly, then balance before tackling.

commonErrors.error: The team remains compressed after regaining possession.
commonErrors.correction: Spread immediately into attacking lanes.

progressions: Increase the size and speed of the possession phase.
Create turnovers closer to either scoring end.
Reduce the time available to regain possession.
Add a full-ground continuation after escape or regain.
Introduce scoreboard consequences for central exits.
regressions: Announce the turnover before it occurs.
Limit escape options to one gate.
Pause after the turnover to organise counter-pressure roles.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor and deepest threat.
Force stoppages, backward movement or regains.
Spread effectively after winning possession back.
matchApplication: Strong teams often regain possession quickly because they compress space immediately after losing the football. This simulation develops that collective counter-pressure response.
relatedDrills: MS-053 – Ground-Level Forward Pressure Wave Simulation

title: Defensive Stoppage Survival Simulation
primarySkill: Defending repeated stoppages close to goal.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to defend repeated stoppages near goal, deny clean opposition exits and create a safe territorial release when possession is won.
groundSize: Inside defensive 50 and approximately 25 metres outside the arc.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position rucks, inside midfielders, forwards and defenders around a stoppage inside defensive 50.
Prepare starting positions for boundary throw-ins and ball-ups.
Set a score and time scenario.
The attacking team attempts to score from repeated stoppages.
The defending team attempts to win possession, force a neutral result or clear beyond the arc.
Play may include multiple consecutive stoppages.
Rotate ruck and midfield combinations.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a stoppage 20–40 metres from goal.
Both teams contest the ruck and first possession.
The attacking team attempts to create an immediate scoring opportunity.
The defending team protects goal-side and central space.
If another stoppage occurs, players reorganise immediately.
If the defending team wins possession, it attempts to clear beyond the defensive-50 arc.
Award the attacking team three points for a goal and one point for a behind.
Award the defending team two points for forcing three consecutive neutral stoppages.
Award three defensive points for a controlled clearance beyond 50.
End after a score, controlled clearance or four stoppages.
coachingPoints: Defensive-side and goal-side roles must be established before the restart.
The ruck should prioritise neutralisation when a clean defensive hit is unavailable.
Midfielders must protect the dangerous exit lane.
Defenders should remain connected to opponents without losing awareness of the ball.
Players must reorganise quickly after each whistle.
A boundary clearance may be safer than forcing central possession.
The team should understand whether conceding a behind is acceptable in the scenario.
Communication must include score, time and stoppage plan.

commonErrors.error: Players line up ball side of opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Establish goal-side and defensive-side position before the restart.

commonErrors.error: The ruck attempts a risky hit in front of goal.
commonErrors.correction: Neutralise the contest when a controlled hit is unavailable.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders all attack the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one player protecting the dangerous release lane.

commonErrors.error: Players argue or relax after another stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Reset roles immediately and prepare for the next restart.

commonErrors.error: Defenders force a central clearance under pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use safe boundary territory when central possession is closed.

progressions: Reduce the time remaining in the scenario.
Begin with the defending team trailing or leading narrowly.
Add one attacking player around the stoppage.
Conceal the exact remaining time.
Continue play to the opposite goal after a defensive clearance.
regressions: Use equal or reduced attacking numbers.
Pause before each stoppage to organise roles.
successIndicators: Manage the scoreboard and time scenario.
matchApplication: Repeated stoppages close to goal often decide tight matches. This simulation develops the composure and defensive discipline required to survive those situations.

title: Forward-50 Repeat Tackle Chain Simulation
primarySkill: Creating consecutive legal tackle and pressure actions inside attacking 50.
objective: Develop the forward group’s ability to continue pressure after the first tackle attempt, close the next receiver and convert repeat defensive actions into scoring opportunities.
groundSize: Inside attacking 50.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position defenders with possession inside defensive 50.
Position forwards in a connected pressure structure.
Mark central and wide defensive exit gates.
Begin with a defender receiving a ground ball or handball under pressure.
The defensive team attempts to complete an exit chain.
The forwards attempt to tackle, force a rushed disposal or regain possession.
Rotate first pressure, cover and interceptor roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach releases the football to a defender.
The nearest forward closes and attempts a legal tackle or pressure action.
If the football is released, the next forward pressures the receiver.
Other forwards guard central and wide exits.
The chain continues until the defenders exit, turn the football over or create a stoppage.
Award the forward team one point for each effective pressure action.
Award three points for a tackle or turnover that produces a goal.
Award two points for forcing a stoppage inside 50.
Award the defensive team three points for a controlled exit.
Reset with a different starting defender and pressure angle.
coachingPoints: Tacklers must close under control and protect their head.
The first pressure player should direct the ball carrier toward support.
The next forward must anticipate the likely release.
Players should complete tackles legally and avoid sling actions.
Support forwards must guard dangerous exits rather than spectate.
Players who miss a tackle must recover into the next pressure action.
After a turnover, the team should spread enough to create a quality scoring option.
Communication must identify pressure, cover and free opponents.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Direction created by the first pressure player.
Quality of the scoring decision after a regain.

commonErrors.error: Tacklers arrive too fast and are evaded.
commonErrors.correction: Decelerate, balance and close the ball carrier’s space.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the football rather than the next receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Anticipate where the disposal is likely to go.

commonErrors.error: Missed tacklers remain on the ground or stop.
commonErrors.correction: Regain feet immediately and join the next pressure action.

commonErrors.error: Tackles become unsafe under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce legal technique and reduce intensity when control is lost.

commonErrors.error: Players rush the scoring disposal after a turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and identify the best scoring option.

progressions: Increase defensive support numbers.
Reduce the size of the exit area.
Begin with the forwards temporarily outnumbered.
Add repeated possessions without reset.
Introduce a scoreboard condition requiring a goal.
regressions: Limit defensive exits to one side.
Begin with a known first receiver.
Pause between pressure actions to coach roles.
successIndicators: Direct the ball carrier toward support.
Force stoppages, turnovers or rushed exits.
Convert pressure wins into quality scoring chances.
matchApplication: Forward pressure often requires several consecutive tackle and chase efforts. This simulation develops the connected pressure chain needed to prevent defensive exits.
relatedDrills: MS-053 – Ground-Level Forward Pressure Wave Simulation

title: Broken-Play Chaos Recovery Simulation
primarySkill: Restoring team roles and structure during unpredictable broken play.
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify the current match phase, assume an effective role and restore team structure when play becomes disorganised.
groundSize: Two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams without fixed starting positions for every repetition.
Place footballs with coaches at several locations.
Begin scenarios using smothered kicks, loose footballs, deflections, missed marks, double turnovers or umpire play-on calls.
Players must identify possession status and organise themselves.
Use normal scoring at each end.
Allow play to continue for 45–75 seconds.
Rotate starting locations and player densities.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with an unpredictable broken-play situation.
Players react without a nominated possession team.
The nearest players contest or secure the football.
Other players identify support, pressure, width, depth and defensive-cover roles.
Once possession is established, the team attacks the appropriate goal.
If another turnover occurs, play continues.
Award three points for a goal.
Award two behaviour points for restoring recognisable team structure within eight seconds.
Award one point for forcing a safe stoppage when possession cannot be established.
Reset after a score, controlled exit or time expiry.
coachingPoints: Players must identify who has possession before choosing their role.
The nearest player contests or pressures while others organise around the play.
Teams should restore width, depth and defensive coverage quickly.
Players must communicate the new attacking direction and dangerous opponents.
A safe stoppage may be preferable to an uncontrolled release.
Ball winners should avoid disposing blindly from chaos.
Players behind the football should delay opposition counterattack.
Once structure returns, the team should play with normal tactical discipline.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Role selection away from the football.
Communication of attacking direction and threats.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs toward the loose football.
commonErrors.correction: Nearest contests while others provide support and coverage.

commonErrors.error: Players attack the wrong direction after possession changes.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate the scoring direction immediately.

commonErrors.error: Ball winners dispose without identifying a teammate.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and scan before releasing.

commonErrors.error: Team width disappears during chaos.
commonErrors.correction: Outside players must restore width once possession becomes clearer.

commonErrors.error: Players continue chaotic play after structure could be restored.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish normal roles and tactical discipline quickly.

progressions: Introduce multiple consecutive broken-play starts.
Reduce coach communication.
Add temporary numerical imbalances.
Use late-game scoreboard conditions.
Play the final block without stoppages other than scores.
regressions: Reduce player numbers and ground size.
Use only one type of broken-play start.
Pause after possession is established to organise roles.
successIndicators: Allocate contest, support and cover roles.
Choose safe possession or stoppage outcomes.
Return to organised football after chaotic phases.
matchApplication: Matches regularly contain deflections, smothers, missed marks and rapid turnovers. This simulation develops the adaptability needed when planned structures temporarily disappear.

title: Wet-Weather Territory Contest Simulation
primarySkill: Managing possession and territory in wet or slippery conditions.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to adapt its skill execution and tactical decisions to wet-weather football while maintaining safety, territory and contest discipline.
groundSize: A corridor or half-ground area approximately 90–120 metres long.
equipment: Safe water application if conditions are dry
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Inspect the surface and remove any unsafe areas before beginning.
Use naturally wet footballs or safely dampen footballs rather than creating a slippery playing surface.
Mark territory lines through a half-ground channel.
Position two teams for live contest and transition.
Begin with ground balls, low kicks, bouncing entries and boundary stoppages.
The teams attempt to gain territory and create scoring opportunities.
Rotate starting positions and contest types.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a wet or slippery football in a contested situation.
Players compete using adjusted ground-ball and body-position techniques.
The team winning possession decides whether to retain, handball, kick for territory or force a stoppage.
Play continues through spills and repeat contests.
Award two points for crossing a territory line.
Award three points for a controlled scoring opportunity.
Award one point for creating a forward stoppage.
Award the opposition two points for intercepting a risky central disposal.
Continue for 45–60 seconds.
Reset with a different wet-weather scenario.
coachingPoints: Players should keep their body behind low footballs.
Possession may require two hands, lowered body position and strong protection.
Short handballs should be used only when the receiver has clear space.
Territory is often more valuable than risky possession.
Kicks should be lower and directed toward safe ground or the boundary.
Players must anticipate spills and second contests.
Tackling and contact intensity should reflect the surface conditions.
Coaches must stop or modify the drill if footing becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Decision between possession, territory and stoppage.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt one-handed gathers.
commonErrors.correction: Use two hands and place the body behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Short handballs are forced into congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Kick for territory or absorb the tackle when no receiver is clear.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt high-risk central kicks.
commonErrors.correction: Use lower, safer kicks toward space or the boundary.

commonErrors.error: Players expect clean possession.
commonErrors.correction: Prepare immediately for spills and secondary contests.

commonErrors.error: Contact remains too aggressive on a slippery surface.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce speed and contact to maintain safe body control.

progressions: Add scoreboard scenarios requiring territory or possession.
Begin from defensive and attacking wet-weather stoppages.
Increase decision pressure without increasing unsafe contact.
Continue play through multiple spills.
Require players to communicate the selected territory plan.
successIndicators: Select territory, possession or stoppage appropriately.
matchApplication: Wet-weather football requires tactical and technical adjustment. This simulation develops safer possession techniques, stronger territory awareness and realistic expectations of repeated contests.

title: Consecutive Contest Resilience Simulation
primarySkill: Maintaining role discipline and effort through consecutive contested phases.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to remain composed, maintain clear roles and execute effective actions through several consecutive contests without a complete reset.
groundSize: Half to two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Prepare four contest starting points across the playing area.
Start with a stoppage, aerial contest, ground ball or pressured possession.
When one contest concludes, the coach immediately introduces the next football at another location.
Players must transition and reorganise without returning to preset positions.
Use blocks containing four to six consecutive contests.
Rotate initial field positions between blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach starts the first contested phase.
Players compete until one team establishes possession or creates a stoppage.
The coach immediately introduces the next football at another location.
Players transition to the new contest according to their current field position.
Teams must allocate contest, support, pressure and defensive-cover roles.
The sequence continues through four to six footballs.
Award one point for winning each contest.
Award one bonus point for maintaining correct structure around the next contest.
Award three points for scoring from the final phase.
Review role discipline and effort after each block.
coachingPoints: Players must complete the current action before transitioning to the next contest.
Not every player should attack each new football.
The closest suitable players contest while others provide support and cover.
Communication should identify who is going and who is holding.
Emotional response to losing one contest must not affect the next action.
Players must continue using safe technique as fatigue builds.
The team should recognise when possession has been established and spread.
Coaches should stop the block if contact or movement quality becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Role allocation at each new contest.
Communication between contest and cover players.
Emotional response after losing a contest.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs to each new football.
commonErrors.correction: Closest suitable players contest while others support and protect structure.

commonErrors.error: Players leave the current contest before it is resolved.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the tackle, disposal or defensive action first.

commonErrors.error: Losing a contest causes frustration or reduced effort.
commonErrors.correction: Treat every new football as a separate opportunity.

commonErrors.error: Communication disappears as fatigue increases.
commonErrors.correction: Call contest, support and hold roles early.

commonErrors.error: Skill and contact technique become unsafe.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce load or finish the block when quality breaks down.

progressions: Increase the number of consecutive contests.
Reduce transition time between footballs.
Add scoreboard consequences for the final phase.
Include uneven numbers at selected contests.
Remove coach location calls and use visual football release only.
regressions: Announce the next contest location early.
Use smaller teams and a reduced area.
successIndicators: Allocate contest, support and cover roles.
Maintain safe technique through repeated effort.
matchApplication: Matches contain long passages involving several contests without a stoppage or reset. This simulation develops the resilience and role discipline required throughout those demanding phases.

title: Pressure and Contest Development Stage Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating advanced pressure, contest, recovery and resilience behaviours across continuous match phases.
objective: Assess whether the team can independently apply the advanced pressure and contest behaviours developed in MS-041 to MS-059 during continuous, varied and physically demanding match simulation.
groundSize: Two-thirds to full ground.
equipment: Towels and spare dry footballs if wet-weather conditions are included
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams with interchange players.
Prepare six scenario cards covering defensive siege, long defensive exit, forward pressure, midfield turnover, defensive stoppage and broken play.
Include one block using a damp football or wet-weather decision constraints if conditions are safe.
Assign coaches specific pressure and contest behaviours to assess.
Establish a scoreboard and countdown clock.
Play three blocks of ten to twelve minutes.
Use short player-led reviews between blocks.
Maintain normal match rules and safe contact standards.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the first starting scenario.
Teams organise and begin live play.
Once the initial phase ends, play continues normally.
Coaches assess pressure angles, contest roles, recovery positioning, communication and decision quality.
At unpredictable moments, the coach introduces a new scenario through a restart or replacement football.
Teams must adapt without a full tactical reset.
At the end of each block, players complete a two-minute review identifying one strength and one priority correction.
Award points for normal match scoring and nominated pressure behaviours.
The final block includes consecutive contest phases under accumulated fatigue.
Conclude with individual, line and team ratings against the success indicators.
coachingPoints: Pressure must protect dangerous space and influence the next disposal.
Players around contests must maintain distinct roles.
Defensive teams must reset quickly during repeated opposition entries.
Long exits require aerial and ground-level organisation.
Counter-pressure must begin immediately after turnovers.
Repeated tackling must remain legal and technically sound.
Players must identify and restore structure during broken play.
Territory and stoppages may be valuable outcomes in difficult conditions.
Fatigue must not remove communication or tactical discipline.
Coaches should assess consistency across the entire session rather than isolated highlights.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Adaptation to wet or difficult footballs.

commonErrors.error: Players apply pressure individually without team connection.
commonErrors.correction: Coordinate the first pressure action with coverage of the next options.

commonErrors.error: Contest numbers arrive without defined responsibilities.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate ball-winner, protector, receiver, pressure and cover roles.

commonErrors.error: Defensive structure fails after repeated efforts.
commonErrors.correction: Reset goal-side, corridor and exit responsibilities after every phase.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue creates rushed disposals or unsafe contact.
commonErrors.correction: Simplify decisions and reduce load when technique deteriorates.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to adapt when conditions or scenarios change.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the current phase and adjust possession, territory and risk.

progressions: Play a full quarter without coach interruption.
Use hidden tactical objectives for each team.
Reduce interchange availability.
Add final-minute scoreboard and time pressure.
Record the assessment for detailed line and player review.
regressions: Use four scenarios rather than six.
Provide player leaders with contest-role reminder cards.
successIndicators: Reset defensive structure during repeated entries.
Organise aerial and ground-level exit support.
Select possession, territory or stoppage appropriately.
Maintain technique and communication under fatigue.
Adapt to changing conditions and scenarios.
Perform pressure and contest behaviours without continuous coach direction.
matchApplication: This assessment completes the pressure-and-contest development stage of the Match Simulation chapter. It determines whether players can transfer contest structure, defensive resilience, forward pressure, turnover response and fatigue discipline into continuous match-like football.MS-061 – Defensive-Half Possession Launch Simulation
relatedDrills: MS-052 – High-Ball Defensive Exit Contest Simulation
MS-053 – Ground-Level Forward Pressure Wave Simulation

title: Defensive-Half Possession Launch Simulation
primarySkill: Launching structured team ball movement from controlled possession in the defensive half.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to establish controlled possession in the defensive half, create multiple exit options and connect effectively with midfield before accelerating into attack.
groundSize: Defensive goal line to approximately 20 metres beyond the centre of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team in possession across defensive 50 and half-back.
Organise the opposition in a realistic forward-half press.
Position midfielders and high forwards beyond defensive 50.
Mark two wide exit gates and one central connection gate near the centre.
Begin each repetition with a defender taking a mark, free kick or uncontested possession.
The possession team attempts to move through the defensive and midfield lines under control.
The pressing team attempts to force a turnover and score.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defensive team begins with controlled possession inside defensive 50.
Teammates immediately spread into short, lateral, long and behind-support positions.
The team circulates the football until it identifies a viable exit.
Once possession crosses defensive 50, midfielders adjust to provide the next connection.
The team attempts to cross one of the midfield gates under control.
Award three points for a central midfield connection.
Award two points for a controlled wide exit followed by retained possession.
Award the pressing team three points for a turnover and scoring opportunity.
Continue until a successful midfield connection, score, turnover or stoppage.
Reset with a different starting defender and pressing structure.
coachingPoints: Defensive players must create width and depth immediately.
The first possession should improve the next player’s angle.
Short options should move the opposition rather than merely accumulate possessions.
The far side must remain occupied throughout the sequence.
Midfielders should adjust their position as the defensive angle changes.
The team should recognise the moment to change from controlled possession to faster attack.
Players behind the football must remain connected against turnover.
Communication should identify switch, corridor and long-target opportunities.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Quality and purpose of short possessions.
Midfield movement in response to the ball.

commonErrors.error: Defenders remain flat across the same line.
commonErrors.correction: Create short, medium and long options at different depths.

commonErrors.error: Short possession does not move the opposition.
commonErrors.correction: Change angle or side with each controlled disposal.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders stand still and wait for the football.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust continuously to the defensive ball movement.

commonErrors.error: The team accelerates before the press is displaced.
commonErrors.correction: Retain possession until a clear exit appears.

commonErrors.error: All players move forward after crossing defensive 50.
commonErrors.correction: Keep connected support behind the football.

progressions: Allow the pressing team to change structures during the repetition.
Require the possession team to continue to a full forward entry.
Reduce the decision time after each mark.
Begin with the defensive team temporarily outnumbered.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios requiring either possession or speed.
regressions: Pause after the first two disposals to coach structure.
successIndicators: Establish width and depth from defensive possession.
Move the opposition with purposeful ball use.
Change tempo when space becomes available.
Protect against turnover throughout the launch.
matchApplication: Controlled defensive possession must eventually connect to midfield and attacking transition. This simulation develops the full launch phase rather than treating the defensive exit as complete once the football leaves defensive 50.
relatedDrills: MS-042 – Pressured Defensive Exit Chain Simulation

title: Wing-to-Corridor Transfer Simulation
primarySkill: Transferring possession from a wide wing position into safe central access.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to retain possession along the wing, move the opposition and enter the corridor through a controlled receiver at the correct moment.
groundSize: From defensive wing to attacking 50 across approximately two-thirds of a ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark one wide wing lane, a central corridor and an attacking target area.
Position one team in possession on the wing.
Organise the opposition to pressure the boundary side and protect the corridor.
Position central midfielders and high forwards as potential transfer receivers.
Include support behind the football.
The possession team attempts to create a controlled central transfer before attacking.
The defending team attempts to intercept and counterattack.
howTheDrillWorks:
The possession team begins with a mark or controlled possession on the wing.
Players use short and lateral movement to shift the opposition.
Central receivers adjust their position to create an angled entry.
The ball carrier enters the corridor only when the receiver has time and a next option.
The corridor receiver releases forward, laterally or back to the wing according to pressure.
Play continues to an inside-50 entry.
Award three points for a corridor transfer followed by a scoring shot.
Award two points for entering and exiting the corridor under control.
Award the defending team three points for a corridor intercept.
Reset from the opposite wing.
coachingPoints: The corridor must be created before it is used.
Central receivers should arrive on an angle rather than stand directly inside the football.
The receiver must scan before possession arrives.
Wing players should retain behind and lateral support.
The football should enter centrally at speed once the opportunity appears.
